Closing Remarks by Dr Adham Ismail, officer in charge WHO Eastern Mediterranean: Progress report on health issues facing populations affected by disasters and emergencies, including implementation of the International Health Regulations (2005)
articles.content: On behalf of the Regional Director, thank you to the Secretariat for this report, and to Member States for your interventions. What this report makes clear is that our Region’s emergency landscape is not easing — it is becoming more complex. Fourteen graded emergencies, eight of them at the highest grade: more than a third of the global total. Protracted conflicts, recurrent outbreaks, climate shocks, and relentless attacks on health care are converging with a shrinking funding envelope. Our emergency response remains more than 40% underfunded against a requirement of US$ 633 million. In 2025, funding constraints hit 1,950 WHO-supported health facilities — more than half suspended operations, affecting 25.9 million people across seven countries. We cannot manage this by continuing to lurch from one crisis to the next. We have to build something more durable. That means, first, sustaining investment in IHR (2005) implementation — particularly at points of entry, in laboratory systems, and in chemical and radiation event readiness, where capacity gaps remain widest. Second, it means embedding collaborative surveillance and public health intelligence, including the responsible use of AI, as standard practice across the Region. Third, it means an uncompromising stance on the protection of health care. In the first half of this year, the Region accounted for nearly half of all WHO-verified incidents worldwide. Health workers, patients, and facilities cannot continue to bear the cost of conflicts they did not start. And fourth, it means shifting toward national ownership and resilience — building recovery into planning from the outset, and replacing appeals made crisis by crisis with sustainable, flexible financing. None of this is the Secretariat’s task alone. It requires sustained political commitment from this Committee, and the Secretariat stands ready to support every Member State in turning that commitment into practice. We know the model delivers: in Somalia, cholera deaths fell from 135 to nine in a single year.

articles.title: Tigers catcher Dillon Dingler wins second straight Gold Glove
articles.content: ST. LOUIS (AP) — First basemen Christian Walker of Houston and Matt Olson of Atlanta won their fourth Gold Gloves on Sunday while Boston right fielder Wilyer Abreu won the fielding honor for the third year in a row and Tigers catcher Dillon Dingler won his second straight. The Red Sox and Arizona tied for the high with three Gold Glove winners each. Red Sox center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela earned the honor for the second straight season and third baseman Caleb Durbin was a first-time winner. Diamondbacks catcher Gabriel Moreno won his second Gold Glove, his first since 2023, while shortstop Geraldo Perdomo and right fielder Corbin Carroll were first-time winners. Walker added to Gold Gloves he won in 2022, ‘23 and ’24. Olson also earned the honor in 2018, ‘19 and ’25. Braves utility man Mauricio Dubón won his third Gold Glove after 2023 and ’25. Other second-time winners included Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman and center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong; New York Yankees left fielder Cody Bellinger; and Milwaukee second baseman Brice Turang. Additional first-time winners included Cleveland pitcher Tanner Bibee; Milwaukee left fielder Jackson Chourio; Texas utility man Ezequiel Duran; New York Mets pitcher Nolan McLean; Tampa Bay shortstop Tanner Walls’ and Seattle second baseman Cole Young. Voting was conducted among managers and up to six coaches from each team, who can’t select players on their own club. Since 2013, voting has been factored with a Society for American Baseball Research defensive index, which comprises about 25% of the total. The utility category is based on a SABR formula and additional defensive statistics. Walker earned a $75,000 bonus for winning the honor, Bibee $50,000 and Turang $25,000.

60 Minutes Transcript: Candidates Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers on the Michigan Senate race
articles.content: This Tuesday, control of the U.S. Senate may be decided in the battleground state of Michigan. The Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, could be the nation's first Muslim senator, and he's running on transformation – busting monopolies, "Medicare For All," an arms embargo on Israel. The Republican candidate, former congressman Mike Rogers, is eager to paint his opponent as a radical – but on policy, he tries to stay inside state lines, focused on Michigan jobs and education. The test for Rogers is whether a Republican can win in the shadow of inflation, war and president Donald Trump's unpopularity. The test for El-Sayed is whether ideas that thrill the progressive wing of the Democratic party are what Middle America wants right now. The contest is close, contentious and it's left the two men without a kind word to say about each other.In the home stretch of an expensive, bruising, and consequential Senate race, we went to speak to both candidates – and see them in action.The son of Egyptian immigrants, Abdul El-Dayed won the Democratic primary against a more centrist rival by a sliver of a percentage point. But he has big ambitions – not just to beat the Republican party, but to remake his own.After a Rhodes Scholarship and a medical degree from Columbia University, El-Sayed went straight into public health administration and then politics.He's often associated with the Democratic Socialists of America – but he isn't a member, and he keeps his distance from the label.Ross Douthat: Pick one economic issue that you think should be the priority for the next Congress.Abdul El-Sayed: Monopolies and oligopolies. I'm a capitalist. If you read Adam Smith, he'll tell you the biggest risk to capitalism was never government regulation. It was always monopoly and oligopoly. Ross Douthat: You ran for office-- in 2018?Abdul El-Sayed: Uh-huh.Ross Douthat: Right? For the first time. You were endorsed by Bernie Sanders in that race. Were you ever a socialist?Abdul El-Sayed: No. I'm a capitalist who understands the idea that you should have guaranteed healthcare in the country, anybody who tells you that's anti-capitalist is not really understanding how capitalism works. El-Sayed is promising a version of Medicare For All that he says would leave private health insurance options intact. He would fund it, in part, with a sweeping tax on billionaire wealth.On the trail, though, he says healthcare is no longer voters' top concern.Ross Douthat: What is the most important issue that you hear about from Michigan voters in this campaign? Pick one.Abdul El-Sayed: I think right now we are barreling toward a world where the most important issue I hear about every day is AI. Ross Douthat: Tell me about that.Abdul El-Sayed: It comes in-- in two different ways. One is students saying, "So I just took $60,000 in loans and the job that I was supposed to have on the back end doesn't exist anymore or might not exist in ten years." Or it's folks in rural communities who say, "They're trying to put a data center in my backyard. I already can't afford my utilities and I'm worried about what it's going to mean for our water." El-Sayed wants a Cabinet-level agency to regulate AI. And for the frontier AI research that some fear threatens the human race …Ross Douthat: Full on pause?Abdul El-Sayed: Full on pause.Where the 42-year-old Democrat sometimes sounds like a candidate for president, his Republican rival Mike Rogers is trying to keep things local. Michigan hasn't elected a republican to the Senate in decades. Rogers hopes to make that a virtue.Mike Rogers: This is a change election in Michigan. And that's why I don't really care what's happening (LAUGH) around the country. I need to fix Michigan.In a populist era, Rogers can sound like a throwback Republican. A former Army officer and FBI agent, he left Congress after 14 years just as Donald Trump ascended. And his platform sometimes channels the compassionate conservative rhetoric of president George W. Bush.Ross Douthat: So what's the number one piece of legislation you'd want to work on on a bipartisan basis if you were in the Senate?Mike Rogers: Reading. Literacy. I'm a big military family. My father, my brother, me, our son is fourth generation. Patriotism runs deep in our family. One of the big reasons they were missing recruiting during COVID and other places was that kids weren't reading well enough to pass the test in America in 2026. If we don't change that, we are all in trouble. When El-Sayed recently took a bus tour with Democratic Socialist star Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez through Trump country in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, they weren't talking about literacy...Abdul El-Sayed: "Shouldn't be this hard in the richest, most powerful country in the history of the world to afford a tank of gas"While the Democrat woos MAGA voters, the 63-year old Rogers has been going into predominantly Black neighborhoods that rarely see a republican, trying to persuade African Americans that El-Sayed is taking them for granted. Mike Rogers at campaign event: "He went to New York with AOC to talk about how they're going to change the world in 2028. You know what I want to do? I wanna take care of Flint. I wanna take care of every Michigander who has kids and grandkids who want to stay in this state."For his pitch to work, Michigan voters have to believe that a Republican senator can fix a Republican president's policies. Trump's trade wars – especially the tariffs on Canada, Michigan's neighbor and trading partner – have cost the state an estimated $23 billion since January 2025.Mike Rogers: I don't like the Canadian tariffs. I've said so. I've, you know, raised my concerns to the secretary of-- commerce.Ross Douthat: And what did he say?Mike Rogers: "I'll get back to ya."Ross Douthat: Why can't other Republican senators fix it, though? There's a Republican Senate majority. Why can't they get the White House to change course?Mike Rogers: Well, you need one more Republican senator there. That's how you do it.Ross Douthat: Would you support, as a Republican senator, trying to override the president on tariffs that you disagree with like the Canadian tariffs?Mike Rogers: If I can't work it out-- and it came to that, yeah. Absolutely. One of El-Sayed's attack lines is that a vote for Rogers is effectively a vote for Trump.The Republican candidate seems to be looking for daylight with the president while avoiding direct confrontation. He supported the unpopular war with Iran. But now says it needs to, quote, "wind" down. When it comes to another issue on voters' minds this fall, Rogers chooses his words carefully.Ross Douthat: Do you think that the Trump administration has a corruption problem?Mike Rogers: Well, I can tell you this. I'm-- I-- I'm an FBI agent by training.Ross Douthat: And what did you work on as an FBI agent?Mike Rogers: Organized crime and public corruption.Ross Douthat: And public corruption. Yes.Mike Rogers: Yeah. Yeah.Ross Douthat: Yes.Mike Rogers: So-- I'm gonna act as a United States senator with the best interests of Michigan. I can tell you that right now.Ross Douthat: Can you tell me a little bit more about what that would mean?Mike Rogers: I'll take the facts as I see them and I'll make a decision based on that.Ross Douthat: The president of the United States accepted a jet from a Middle Eastern nation. Do you think he should have done that?Mike Rogers: I mean, that's not what I would have done. But that's-- I don't think it's illegal for the president to do that. It's a delicate relationship. President Trump needs Rogers to flip the seat. Rogers needs the president to turn out the party base. They campaigned together in Port Huron, Michigan, last week, where Mr. Trump trained his fire on El-Sayed.President Trump at rally: "I'm here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator."The president is talking about an Islamist movement whose offshoots were recently designated as terrorist groups. Rogers has also accused his opponent of having links to the Muslim Brotherhood, citing a 2012 letter that El-Sayed signed after the Arab Spring in support of Egypt's new democratically elected government, which was backed by the Brotherhood.El-Sayed has declined to comment on the letter but says he disavows the Muslim Brotherhood. He argues that Republicans are targeting his Islamic faith.Ross Douthat: There's a lot of people, Muslim, Christian, otherwise, who are raised in religion and it doesn't stick. Why did faith stick for you?Abdul El-Sayed: I think anybody of faith has on again, off again relationships with one's own faith. In my younger years, I certainly rebelled. And it was something that-- that kinda came back to me in college.Ross Douthat: Tell me something about how that faith shapes your politics.Abdul El-Sayed: There is this-- notion of speak the truth, even if it be against yourself. And I try to be, like, radically honest. One place where El-Sayed casts himself as a truth-teller is the debate over U.S. support for Israel. Ross Douthat: In your view, what's wrong with America's relationship with Israel?Abdul El-Sayed: Number one, we have been told that we are pursuing a two-state solution, only to aid, arm, and abet the very people who are trying to foreclose on the possibility of a second state. So it's incoherent on its own terms. Number two, I don't know about you, but I don't pay my taxes to buy another country a bomb or a tank. That's Israel. That's Egypt. That's Saudi Arabia. That's Pakistan. Three, the state of Israel did a genocide.Mike Rogers: His language is wrong. They use terms like genocide.In the argument over Israel's war in Gaza, following the October 7th attacks by Hamas, Rogers leaves no doubt which side he's on.Mike Rogers: I passionately defend Israel's right to defend itself and to exist as a Jewish state. That sets me at odds with my opponent right off the bat. He refuses to even acknowledge that Israel has the right to exist. Abdul El-Sayed: I don't ever get the question of, "Does Palestine have the right to exist?"Ross Douthat: Does Palestine have the right to exist?Abdul El-Sayed: Yes.Ross Douthat: Does Israel have--Abdul El-Sayed: And--Ross Douthat: --the right to exist?Abdul El-Sayed: S-- yes. If there is a shared understanding--Ross Douthat: Wait. You said-- you said--Abdul El-Sayed: Let me just-- let me just-- let me just-- understand. I believe-- and this is the-- this is the problem with this debate. We start from where we sit rather than start from principles. I believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike. If the Palestinian people decide and the Israeli people decide that they want two states for two people, and they decide that on equal terms, I'm for it. If they decide that they want one state shared in a different way, I'm for that. In a state with one of the nation's largest Arab American populations – and about 100,000 Jewish voters – the Middle East is territory where the campaign's national and local elements converge.This past March, after a terrorist attack on a Michigan synagogue and preschool, El-Sayed condemned the violence.Abdul El-Sayed video: "There is never a justification for attacking innocent people or houses of worship. articles.title: Election Day — and results — draws near
articles.content: Nine days of early in-person voting in Michigan came to an end on Sunday, Nov. 1. Early voting sites were open since Oct. 24. According to the Michigan Secretary of State, voters have returned 1,704,715 ballots in advance of the Nov. 3 election as of Friday, Oct. 30. That’s 23% of the registered voters in the state. Voters will head to the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3, with gubernatorial, U.S. Senate and U.S. House races highlighting this year’s midterm election. The ballot will also contain state House and Senate races, as well as statewide proposals, city council and township board races, and municipal and school district proposals, will also appear on ballots across the area. Two Macomb County politicians are seeking higher office, including Republican U.S. Rep. John James who faces Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson for governor. Also, Macomb County’s clerk/register of deeds Anthony Forlini, a Republican, is going up against Michigan Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist, a Democrat, as they seek the secretary of state’s position. No matter when a Michigan voting ballot is turned in, none are tabulated by local election clerks until after the polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 3. Voters can cast their ballots in person on Election Day or can return absentee ballot to drop boxes, local clerk’s office, or polling place.

Trump launches racist diatribe against Abdul El-Sayed at Iowa rally
articles.content: President again took aim at progressive Senate candidate and lauded Haley Stevens for endorsing Mike Rogers Donald Trump railed against Democratic US senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign event in Iowa Sunday, repeatedly referring to the Michigan progressive as a “jihadist”. Trump’s comments aimed to influence a neck-and-neck race that will play an outsized role in determining which party controls the senate after Tuesday’s midterm elections. The president bashed El-Sayed, a practicing Muslim, in brazenly racist terms, saying that Congress would have to “get a special metal detector for Abdul” if he were elected. “If you vote for this jihadist lunatic that wants to destroy you, you’re crazy,” Trump said. The Michigan race has drawn national attention in recent days, as Hayley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the August primary election, declined to campaign with him, while demanding that he publicly disavow an outside group’s political ad that posited a link between rising prices and US military support for Israel’s war on Gaza. El-Sayed responded by telling Stevens to stay away from a campaign event at which they were supposed to appear together on Sunday. Stevens turned around and endorsed Mike Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent. Steven’s high-profile defection in the waning hours of the tight race drew the condemnation of Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, who is Jewish. Trump, on the other hand, heaped praise on Stevens for turning against El-Sayed, urging her to join the GOP. “It was an incredible thing,” Trump said. “I’d love her to join the Republican party. I think that could happen.” Trump then lauded Rogers in metaphorical terms. Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk. “Mike Rodgers is apple pie,” Trump said. “And you know what this country needs? A little apple pie. We don’t need the communists or jihadists, the Muslim Brotherhood. We need apple pie. He’s apple pie. He’ll be good.” Trump had little time to watch football this weekend, he noted, because he had been “going to these damn rallies all over the place”. “Pretend I’m on the ballot,” Trump said. “Essentially, I am on the ballot.”

Hochul stumps with Mamdani and AOC during Buffalo Bills NYC watch party ahead of election
articles.content: See more of our coverage in your search results. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul stumped with Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at a Buffalo Bills watch party in Queens Sunday during the last weekend of her campaign, saying the divisive pols “want to be with me.” Hochul was all smiles as she campaigned with the two progressives at Murphy’s Sports Bar in Astoria, and insisted the support of the two controversial lefty figures wouldn’t turn off moderate voters ahead of Tuesday’s gubernatorial election. “They want to support me and I’m grateful to have such a broad base of individuals with different perspectives who are joining our coalition to make sure Democrats win big,” Hochul told reporters. The pair of Democratic socialists kept mum as they left the bar 20 minutes ahead of the incumbent governor, with exiting patrons describing the establishment as half empty in the pols’ presence. “This is the place we come for the games, but this… no,” customer Jose Rodriguez Jr., 39, said. He and his girlfriend left the spot as the politicians campaigned. “We’re just going to go find some other place where we can watch the game,” Rodriguez said. The Democratic governor, who is expected to beat challenger Nassau County executive Bruce Blakeman Tuesday, insisted to reporters that she’s taking the final days of the election “so seriously” as she left the watering hole. “I’m taking this so seriously because what we do here in New York will have an effect on the future of this country,” the incumbent said. She also added her hopes to see a Democratic sweep ahead of the midterm elections in order to “start taking back our country.” “If we make Hakeem Jeffries our speaker, all of a sudden we can just put up a firewall up there and stop the insanity and start taking back our country,” Hochul said. Tuesday’s gubernatorial race has received national attention, even leading to the Queens-raised President Trump calling Hochul “the worst governor in the history of New York State.” “She’s been a disaster, and I can tell you that Bruce has been a friend of mine for a long time,” Trump added at a rally on Saturday, where he implored New Yorkers to vote for the Republican challenger.

articles.title: Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers called a ‘disgrace’ at Detroit unity roundtable
articles.description: Organizers with the Abdul El-Sayed campaign hosted a conversation with Black, Arab and Muslim Americans in Detroit on Sunday afternoon in an effort to unify Democrats in the final stretch before the election. Former U.S. Rep. Jamaal Bowman of New York, state Senate candidate Abbas Alawieh, Michigan United organizer Elder Leslie Matthews and Layla Elabed, […]
articles.content: Supporters of Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed gather for a roundtable of Black, Arab and Muslim Michiganders in Detroit on Nov. 1, 2026. (Photo by Minnah Arshad/Michigan Advance)Organizers with the Abdul El-Sayed campaign hosted a conversation with Black, Arab and Muslim Americans in Detroit on Sunday afternoon in an effort to unify Democrats in the final stretch before the election. Former U.S. Rep. Jamaal Bowman of New York, state Senate candidate Abbas Alawieh, Michigan United organizer Elder Leslie Matthews and Layla Elabed, organizing director of Arab Americans for Progress and a co-founder of the Uncommitted movement, were among the speakers on Sunday afternoon. The invite-only roundtable, moderated by the Women for Abdul coalition and Reproductive Freedom for All Michigan, drew about two dozen people to Haraz Coffee House, a Yemeni cafe in Detroit. It began shortly after U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) withdrew her support for El-Sayed and endorsed Republican nominee Mike Rogers in an 11th-hour announcement that drew widespread condemnation from Democratic Party leaders. Former U.S. Rep. Jamaal Bowman (D-New York) stands between Machhadie Assi (left), the El-Sayed campaign’s deputy director of coalitions, and Dr. Tonya Trotter, at a roundtable of Black, Arab and Muslim Michiganders in Detroit on Nov. 1, 2026. (Photo by Houssam Mchaimech) Bowman, who represented New York’s 16th Congressional District until last year, called Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers a “disgrace” and said she “represents white supremacy.” “This is a reckoning of American democracy. Haley Stevens showed you who she was,” he said. “We can never let white supremacy win. When there is division or hate, it’s rooted in that.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Bowman added that voters can never forget what Stevens did. “The more they keep us believing that we are separate, that we are different, the more they create the economic and social conditions that we are crabs in a barrel fighting to get over each other in lieu of the other, and if we internalize those beliefs, that is the thing that makes us weak,” Bowman said. In the August primary, Stevens performed strongly among Black voters, including in Detroit, where she defeated El-Sayed by 28 percentage points. Her campaign and its supporters, including AIPAC’s super PAC, ran ads tailored to Black voters. The ads had criticized El-Sayed’s support for the Uncommitted movement in the 2024 presidential primary, which was a protest movement over the Biden administration’s handling of Gaza. El-Sayed later endorsed Kamala Harris for president the day after she announced her campaign. From L-R: Former U.S. Rep. Jamaal Bowman (seated), Dr. Tonya Trotter, Catreese Qualls of Women for Abdul and Elder Leslie Mathews (seated), an organizer with Michigan United, attend at a roundtable of Black, Arab and Muslim Michiganders in Detroit on Nov. 1, 2026. (Photo by Houssam Mchaimech) Since then, El-Sayed has sought to win over Black voters in Detroit and across the state, as polls suggest a tight race on Tuesday. El-Sayed will likely need strong turnout among Black Michiganders, a reliably Democratic voting bloc, to defeat Rogers. Word of Stevens’ defection has drawn widespread condemnation from all wings of the Democratic Party. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York), who back Stevens during the primary, called her decision a “despicable betrayal,” while Democratic National Committee Black Caucus Chair Virgie Rollins said Stevens had “revealed herself to be a sellout who used Black Michiganders for a political stunt.” This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens. Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors. — Chuck Schumer (@chuckschumer) November 1, 2026 Alawieh, who cross-endorsed El-Sayed, said at the event on Sunday that he has benefited from “a world where my parents had their full rights, where they had access to economic opportunity,” which he said would not have been possible without the generational sacrifices of Black Americans. He called out anti-Black racism among Arab Americans, including stereotypes he heard as a child that “Black neighborhoods are somehow inherently dangerous.” “There is pain between our communities from where we come from,” he said. “If we’re honest about where the hurt has been, then we can take that next step forward and that next one after that,” Alawieh said. Alawieh also said he’s supporting El-Sayed not “because he looks like me,” but because of the Senate nominee’s policies. “What our communities know more than anyone, and many Black women have taught us this more than anyone, is you don’t need to vote for someone who looks exactly like you in order for your interests to be represented,” Alawieh said. “If the interests of women would be represented best by only a woman candidate, then we would not be living in a world where Haley Stevens so quickly sells out the right to choose, sells out voting rights, sells out health care, just so she can go support a genocide-enabling Mike Rogers.” Elder Leslie Mathews, an organizer with Michigan United, said at the event that she had built relationships with Arab American and Palestinian women in the last three years in her anti-war advocacy for Gaza. Matthews said she was attending the discussion in her personal capacity. Elder Leslie Mathews, an organizer with Michigan United, speaks to supporters of Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed at a roundtable of Black, Arab and Muslim Michiganders in Detroit on Nov. 1, 2026. (Photo by Minnah Arshad/Michigan Advance) “It’s not even about being Black and Arab, but it’s really about being human,” Mathews said. Mathews spoke about the frustration and pain she felt in 2024 over the presidential election, when some Arab Americans, Muslims, and pro-Palestinian supporters declined to back former Vice President Kamala Harris for president over Gaza. “One of the reasons why we lost that election was because we didn’t come together, because I felt that you couldn’t feel my pain, you felt that I couldn’t feel your pain,” Mathews said. Now, Mathews said she hopes to unify Black and brown communities behind a united agenda, and said El-Sayed is “one of the things that we can all fight for.” Layla Elabed, who co-founded the 2024 Uncommitted movement to protest the Biden administration’s handling of Gaza, said Black and brown women are often celebrated as the backbone of democracy “while keeping us out of the places where decisions are made.” “There is a history of Black communities being told that they cannot govern themselves. We experienced this firsthand in Detroit under emergency management,” she said. “These experiences, the lessons I learned, especially as somebody born and raised in Detroit, sometimes the very people who tell you how important your voice is becomes uncomfortable the moment you decide to use it.”

Millages for Detroit Zoo, Museum of African American History, Detroit Historical Society on ballot
articles.description: The Detroit Zoo is seeking a renewal of its millage, and the Charles Wright Museum of African American History and the Detroit Historical Society are seeking their first ever millage.
articles.content: Voters in Oakland, Macomb, and Wayne counties will decide a millage renewal for the Detroit Zoo in the November election.Hayley Murphy is the zoo's Executive Director. She said in addition to the exhibits and care for about 2,000 animals, from 200 species, the zoo operates educational outreach programs for communities and schools, and operates the Belle Isle Nature Center.Murphy said the zoo has been a legacy institution for nearly 100 years. "People tell me 'I was there with my kids because my parents brought me, and their parents brought them.' We also contribute over $190 million annually in our economic impact to the tri-county region," Murphy said.Murphy said the renewal raises money equivalent to a third of the zoo's operating budget.Two other major cultural institutions — The Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History, and the Detroit Historical Society, are seeking approval of their first-ever millage request to sustain their operations.It's on the ballot for voters in Oakland and Wayne counties.Neil Barclay, executive director of the museum, said it's no longer possible to fund the institutions with ticket sales and grants alone.The millage would not just sustain current operations but expand them, he said, allowing both institutions to offer free admission, increase outreach activities, as well as help fund smaller museums and historical societies in the region.Wright said the museum and historical society host more than 20,000 schoolchildren a year."We've seen the transformative power of students coming through these institutions and just beaming — feeling really different about themselves and who they are, where they come from, and how important this city really is in the world," he said.Barclay said a lot is riding on the millage. He said both institutions will have to trim their budgets, and possibly reduce hours, staffing and outreach if the millage does not pass.

articles.description: Police Chief Jennifer Brown provided updates on two shootings and two car-pedestrian crashes in East Lansing Halloween weekend.
articles.content: Two shootings and two vehicle-pedestrian crashes in East Lansing sent people to the hospital on Halloween night and early Sunday morning, Police Chief Jennifer Brown said. At a press conference Sunday afternoon, Brown provided updates on the seven individuals hospitalized in connection to the four incidents. Six of those hospitalized are in stable condition and the condition of the other person is unknown. There is no known threat to the community at this time, Brown said. “On one of our busiest nights, the East Lansing Police Department officers provided life saving aid to gunshot victims, secured multiple crime scenes and removed impaired drivers from our streets,” Brown said. The first shooting took place near the intersection of M.A.C. Avenue and Linden Street early Sunday morning. Three people were hospitalized with gunshot wounds, Brown said. Two are in stable conditions and the status of the third is unknown. Brown did not say if a person was arrested in connection to this shooting. The other shooting unfolded near Frye Avenue and Stoddard Street. Brown said two people were hospitalized with gunshot wounds and are now in stable condition. Brown said “several” individuals were taken into custody and multiple guns were recovered from the scene, though it’s still not known if these were the weapons used in the shooting. There were also two serious car crashes that may have involved impaired drivers. The first car-pedestrian crash occurred on Abbot Road near Library Lane, Brown said. The driver remained at the scene and was arrested under suspicion of operating while intoxicated. The pedestrian has since undergone surgery and is now in stable condition. A second pedestrian was hit by a car at the intersection of Grand River Avenue and Gunson Street. A person was arrested for suspected operating while intoxicated and a firearm was recovered from the vehicle. The victim is in stable condition. Additionally, Brown said that the East Lansing Fire Department responded to 91 incidents over 24 hours, with 75 incidents taking place over night. Brown said the ELPD will be releasing more information as it becomes available and did not take questions after the roughly 4-minute long press conference. articles.title: Haley Stevens endorses Mike Rogers, bucking Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race
articles.description: US Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican US Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday amid tensions with Democratic primary rival Abdul El-Sayed.
articles.content: Democratic US Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers for US Senate and joined him at a church Detroit The endorsement came as Democrats prepared a ‘unity rally’ for Abdul El-Sayed, who beat Stevens in the primary El-Sayed and Rogers are locked in a tight battle for Michigan’s open US Senate seat DETROIT — Democratic US Rep. Haley Stevens on Sunday endorsed Republican Mike Rogers for US Senate, bucking former primary rival Abdul El-Sayed just two days before the Nov. 3 election. “Abdul made very clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn’t need me there, that he didn’t want me there, and at some point, you got to look at who’s standing for country,” Stevens said after joining Rogers at Perfecting Church in Detroit. “We have to stand with country. We can’t stand with hate,” she added, referencing the running feud she has had with El-Sayed over US support for the Israeli government. More fact checks: Rogers backed abortion bans, says he won’t undo Michigan rights Mike Rogers claims Abdul El-Sayed wants an ‘energy tax’ Mike Rogers faces voter suppression claims over Detroit comments Rogers called Stevens’ decision “courage in politics,” characterizing the unlikely political pairing as “a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country than it is anything else.” “Candidly, I’m glad I’m not running against Haley Stevens today,” he told reporters during a Sunday press conference. Stevens’ endorsement came as other Democrats were headed to a separate church event in Detroit in an attempt to present a united front behind El-Sayed in a race that could decide control of the U.S. Senate. Speaking to reporters after the event, El-Sayed said he is focused on fighting for the needs of other Michiganders — not Stevens, who he said he doesn’t think about much. “If you’re somebody who believes that we should stand up to hate, and you have watched this last campaign, I think we probably would not want to support Mike Rogers and Donald Trump and J.D. Vance,” he said. Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks with reporters before a Souls to the Polls campaign event at Northend Church of God in Christ, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) Several fellow Democrats quickly criticized Stevens, including state party Chair Curtis Hertel. He said her decision to campaign with Rogers “shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about. “We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us,” Hertel added. Stevens congressional chief of staff Justin German immediately resigned his post and said “many” other employees in her office had as well. In a statement, he encouraged Michiganders to vote for El-Sayed and “stand up for the America we all believe in.” But Republicans like former national and Michigan GOP Chair Ronna McDaniel praised Stevens for “putting our state before party.” “It takes courage to do this and while some will attack you, just know this is exactly what we need more of in this country,” McDaniel said on social media. How we got here Stevens, who lost in the primary to El-Sayed, was initially set to join the nominee and U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina at the “unity” event. Those plans unraveled after a dispute over Israel and an outside group’s campaign advertisement escalated into a public exchange of criticism between the rivals. Debbie Dingell, the Michigan congresswoman who helped organize the planned joint appearance in hopes of bringing together Democrats in the final days before Tuesday’s vote, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that. “I’m the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting,” Dingell told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.” “The bishop was getting upset, because this is a real church service,” Dingell added. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., left, her fiance Jason Turkish, right, stand with Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, second left, and his wife Kristi Rogers during a church service at Perfecting Church, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Jose Juarez) The latest and late-stage infighting comes as Democrats look to drive turnout among Black and Jewish voters in key strongholds. El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is in a tight race with Mike Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by Democrat Gary Peters, who is retiring. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Republican President Donald Trump’s second term. Dingell and other Democrats insist the party is united behind El-Sayed, who would be the country’s first Muslim senator if elected. Early voting has been underway since Oct. 24, before the latest tensions erupted. But the renewed bickering has complicated Democrats’ efforts to deliver a unified closing message in crucial areas such as Detroit, where turnout could prove decisive. “All you guys want to talk about was Abdul and Haley and it really needs to be about what the issues are that people should be voting about on Tuesday,” Dingell said. She added about El-Sayed’s Republican opponent: “Mike Rogers loved every minute of it.” The tensions carry particular significance in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighboring Oakland County. Stevens defeated El-Sayed in both counties in the August primary, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition. Throughout the primary cycle, Stevens promised to endorse the Democratic nominee and did so following her loss to El-Sayed. Earlier this week, she told CNN she would still vote for El-Sayed after her fiance Jason Turkish, a Jewish Democrat and civil rights attorney, said he planned to vote for Rogers in the general election. Following that announcement, El-Sayed told reporters “there are always going to be some folks who have different opinions, and they’re welcome to that.” “If folks see another issue that is more important to them and decide that their disagreement with me on that is bigger than their disagreement with me on all these other things, that is their choice,” he said. articles.content: Gravity is a cruel mistress, slowly dragging the famed Hubble Space Telescope ever closer to its ultimate demise with every day. Hubble is in no immediate danger of burning up in the Earth’s atmosphere, but its time will run out in the early to mid 2030s unless its orbit is boosted. So NASA is taking proposals from the private sector to see if anyone can save it. In a post on NASA’s site, Administrator Jared Isaacman said: > Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible … If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe. articles.content: Five people were shot and injured in two incidents that happened over a chaotic and busy Halloween night for emergency responders, as East Lansing called in neighboring law enforcement and fire departments to help. East Lansing Police Chief Jennifer Brown at a news conference on Nov. 1, 2026. Photo by Mike Ellis/City Pulse East Lansing Police Chief Jennifer Brown said Sunday that officers are investigating two shootings that happened over the Halloween night, along with two pedestrian crashes and 75 calls overnight for the city’s firefighters, who are also medics. At a news conference called Sunday, Brown said described four of the shooting victims as being in stable condition and officials not knowing the condition of the fifth person. The news conference lasted less than five minutes and after reading a statement at the city’s police station, Brown said she would not take questions from reporters. The first shooting happened near the intersection of MAC Avenue and Linden sometime after midnight, Brown said. The chief did not give a specific time but The State News reported that the shots happened around 12:26 a.m. Brown said three people were treated for gunshot wounds, with the condition of one person being unknown. The second shooting happened at the intersection of Stoddard and Frye avenues in the early morning hours, Brown said. Two people injured in that shooting are in stable condition in a hospital, she said. There’s no ongoing threat to the community at this time, Brown said. East Lansing Police Chief Jennifer Brown at a news conference on Nov. 1, 2026. Photo by Mike Ellis/City Pulse “We are aware that this situation was extremely frightening for our bystanders including Michigan State students as well as their families, our relationship with the university is strong and we will continue to work together. On one of our busiest nights, East Lansing officers provided life saving aid to gunshot victims, secured multiple crime scenes and removed impaired drivers from our streets.” Brown said there were two collisions involving pedestrians and DUI arrests, which overlapped with the shootings. The first collision happened at Abbott Road and Library Lane. The second happened at Grand River and Gunson, and authorities recovered a firearm from the vehicle, Brown said. The pedestrians in both cases are in stable condition, the first having been through surgery Sunday morning, Brown said. She said the city’s fire department handled 91 incidents in 24 hours including 75 overnight. The busy night involved tapping in at least five other law enforcement agencies and several neighboring fire departments for mutual aid, Brown said. She said she was grateful for the assistance and for her own department’s staff, many of whom were called in to help with the various incidents.

articles.title: Michigan race: All you need to know about Abdul El-Sayed vs Mike Rogers
articles.content: Al Jazeera examines the crucial US Senate race in Michigan, including the candidates’ positions and largest spenders. Dearborn, Michigan – Chadi Abdulrazek, an Arab American political activist who has been volunteering to help elect Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, says he’s spoken in recent days to journalists from Denmark, Sweden, the Netherlands, France and the United Kingdom. The United States Senate race between El-Sayed and his Republican rival Mike Rogers is attracting national and international attention, reflecting the potent political symbolism that belies its outcome, which extends far beyond one seat in the upper chamber of the US Congress. Supporters in each camp paint the contest as a crucial fight that could shape the political direction of the state and the US for years to come. Abdulrazek, a small business owner, said the election is a chance to hold Trump accountable for breaking his promises to pursue peace in the world and focus on the needs of Americans. For Arab and Muslim communities that have been facing Islamophobic attacks as part of the Senate race, the vote is pivotal, he added. “What’s on the line is they have to stand up for themselves and say, ‘We are part of this country, and we’re going to be voting, and we will actually make a change’,” Abdulrazek told Al Jazeera. Here, Al Jazeera looks at the US Senate race in Michigan and why it has gained so much attention. El-Sayed is a public health advocate who previously led the health department in Detroit and Wayne County in southeast Michigan. He is 42. If elected, the Democrat of Egyptian descent would become the first-ever Muslim US senator. El-Sayed ran for governor in 2018 but fell short in the Democratic primary against eventual winner Gretchen Whitmer. The Democratic nominee has embraced progressive policies, especially Medicare for All – a plan to expand government-funded healthcare to everyone in the US. Rogers is a 63-year-old former US Congress member and state legislator. The Republican nominee ran for the Senate in 2024 and narrowly lost to centrist Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin. He is a close ally of Donald Trump, but has sought to create some distance between his campaign and the unpopular US president. For example, Rogers has supported Trump’s decision to join Israel in launching the war against Iran, while also calling for an end to the conflict. The Republican candidate also backs tax cuts, increasing domestic energy production and deregulation. It will be difficult for Democrats to gain control of the Senate if they lose Michigan. The seat is currently held by retiring Democrat Gary Peters. A Rogers win would hand the swing state Senate seat to Republicans for at least six years. The race, however, is not just about the partisan math in the Senate. It is a test of the electoral viability of progressive ideas, including sharp criticism of Israel, in a swing state. While the Senate has many progressive members, most come from coastal states considered Democratic strongholds. A victory for El-Sayed in Michigan would show that his message can attract a winning coalition, which could influence how Democratic presidential candidates may go about their campaigning in 2028. There is also the factor of El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, which had become the subject of near-daily attacks by Rogers and Trump. The race has raised questions about whether Michigan and the US are ready for a Muslim senator. It is uncommon for the candidate who lost a primary to be part of a major storyline in the general election, but Stevens has been making headlines days ahead of the vote after her fiance endorsed Rogers, citing El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Stevens, a Democrat in the US House of Representatives, has also criticised El-Sayed for his positions on Israel while saying she would still vote for the Democratic candidate. On Sunday, Stevens took it a step further and appeared with Rogers at a press conference and endorsed the Republican candidate. “I’m choosing country over hate,”she said after attending a church service with Rogers. “This is not anti-Muslim at all.” Democrats immediately spoke out against Stevens, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer calling her actions a “dispicable betrayal”. El-Sayed also hit back, saying he “does not think about Haley Stevens”. El-Sayed has accused Israel of carrying out a genocide in Gaza, echoing the findings of major human rights organisations and United Nations investigators. The Democrat has also linked wars, including the conflict in Iran and US aid to Israel, to domestic issues. He says that US taxpayer money is better spent on addressing issues at home, such as healthcare and crumbling infrastructure. Pro-Israel groups, namely the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), have spent tens of millions of dollars to help defeat El-Sayed. AIPAC backed El-Sayed’s opponent Haley Stevens with more than $30m, making Israel policy one of the most discussed subjects in the election. El-Sayed overcame the spending onslaught in the primaries, but Rogers – a staunch Israel supporter – has seized on the criticism of El-Sayed from pro-Israel advocates, including some Democrats. Rogers – who has pledged unconditional support for Israel – has accused El-Sayed of caring more for Palestine than Michigan. After a lull in spending in Michigan, AIPAC has returned to the race to back Rogers. The pro-Israel lobby group’s election arm, United Democracy Project, has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on mailers against El-Sayed. According to The New York Times, it has funnelled $9m to a Republican group supporting Rogers. Both Rogers and El-Sayed supporters interviewed by Al Jazeera have stressed the race’s importance. Former Democratic state legislator Cynthia Johnson said the negative campaigning around El-Sayed’s religion and ethnicity makes the election especially crucial. “What’s really at stake is life or death. Our children are being exposed to some very negative, nasty things,” Johnson told Al Jazeera. “We have to vote like our lives depended on it because we have a person who’s in the White House right now who’s a maniac and we need as many people who are going to speak up as possible – people like Abdul.” Outside a Trump rally on Sunday, Rogers supporter Rob Cortis expressed similar urgency. “This election is so important. Our country is at stake. Our border is at stake. The future of our children in America is at stake,” Cortis told Al Jazeera. “If it flips to communism, socialism or if it goes to Muslim rule, America was never intended for that. America is intended to be a nation of Christians, showing the goodness of God,” he said. Most recent polls have shown El-Sayed with a narrow lead over Rogers – ranging from four to seven percentage points. However, polling in Michigan – a diverse state of more than 10 million people – has been unreliable over the past decades, often getting the results wrong by several percentage points. The Cook Political Report has classified the race as a toss-up, and both campaigns have warned their supporters that the result may come down to a few thousand votes. With nearly $300m spent, Michigan’s US Senate race is quickly becoming one of the most expensive in the country. Political action committees (PACs) aligned with both major parties have been buying ads in support of their respective candidates. On the Republican side, one of the largest spenders has been Senate Leadership Fund, whose largest donors include pro-Israel billionaire Miriam Adelson. MAGA Inc and its subsidiary No Going Back, a pro-Trump group funded by the US president’s allies, including Adelson and Elon Musk, have also spent millions of dollars on the race. Great Lakes Conservatives Fund (GLCF), a Michigan Republican PAC that AIPAC has backed in general elections, has also been a big spender, according to media reports. The Senate Majority PAC (SMP) and an affiliated group called WINSENATE have been the largest spenders. SMP’s top funders include businessmen Fred Eychaner and Amos Hostetter Jr. Early voting is under way across Michigan, and hundreds of thousands of people have already cast their ballots. Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, will be the last day to vote. Polls in Michigan close at 8pm (01:00 GMT on Wednesday). That depends on how close the race is. If it’s a tight contest, Michigan likely will not find out who won until Wednesday. In the primaries in August, when El-Sayed narrowly defeated Stevens, the Associated Press did not call the race until about 10am (15:00 GMT) on the Wednesday after Election Day. Likewise, Michigan was called for Trump in 2024 around 1pm (18:00 GMT) on the day after the election. However, if one of the candidates acquires a commanding lead across the state, he could be projected as the winner hours after the polls close.

French protest violence eases while scattered riots hit Germany ahead of school return
articles.description: French protest violence eases while scattered riots hit Germany ahead of school return AP News Clashes Erupt Again in France, After Festive Start to Day of Protest The New York Times France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police BBC From teargas in Paris to gen Z in Germany: protests across Europe – in pictures The Guardian Massive protests sweep Europe over cost of living and stra
articles.content: PARIS (AP) — French authorities expressed relief Sunday after mass protests over rising living costs resulted in less violence than previous weekends. But police expect new demonstrations as high schools at the heart of the movement reopen Monday after their autumn break. Germany faced its own challenges after nationwide protests Saturday ended with rioters attacking police and looting stores in some cities. Around Europe, hundreds of thousands joined overwhelmingly peaceful marches Saturday inspired by young people, despite scattered unrest. In Paris, rioters targeted police with Molotov cocktails at the end of Saturday’s march on the city’s eastern edge, injuring three officers and setting a car ablaze, police said. Across town, masked groups hurled fireworks at officers at a viewpoint across from the Eiffel Tower, and police charged repeatedly, sending panicked visitors fleeing the area. Overall, however, the violence was less severe than on Oct. 17, when a city hall was torched and more than 2,000 stores were looted in hours of violence that authorities seemed unprepared to control, or during follow-up protests Oct. 24. Police arrested 779 people Saturday, compared with 2,628 on Oct. 17 and 1,314 last weekend. Paris and Marseille police said a handful of shops were targeted but no major damage was reported. About 70,000 police were deployed around the country. Protesters described various struggles to The Associated Press: with rodents in classrooms, low-wage jobs, putting fuel in their cars. Police are preparing for more tensions as schools reopen Monday, with some groups calling for blockades. Thursday, France is facing a general strike on trains and public services and protests by both students and labor unions demanding higher wages and other measures. French President Emmanuel Macron’s government is focusing on Thursday’s actions and negotiating with unions — a familiar ballet in French politics -- and hoping that the harder-to-control rioting dies down, according to an official close to the president. The official described Saturday’s protests as ″a return to republican order″ but acknowledged the situation is ″not perfect.’' The official was not authorized to be publicly named according to presidential policy. More than 100,000 mostly young people protested peacefully across Germany on Saturday, demanding that the government invest more money in education, housing, climate protection and make daily life more affordable. In some cities the protests turned violent at night. Following a demonstration in Frankfurt, rioters attacked police downtown and looted stores. More than 100 officers were injured and 54 people — aged 13 to 29 — were detained. It wasn’t clear how many of the protesters were injured. Police said 17 stores were damaged and five of those were looted. After police cordoned off an area in the city center, the situation calmed down by early Sunday morning. “I am shocked by the violent excesses in Frankfurt, which will not go unpunished,” said Boris Rhein, the governor of Hesse, where Frankfurt is located. “Anyone who behaves like the attackers in downtown Frankfurt places themselves outside our society.’' Violence also broke out Saturday night in Cologne, where police used water cannons to disperse the crowd. In Berlin, protesters attacked police with bottles and pyrotechnics. The organizers of Saturday’s protests, a youth initiative called “Gen Z regelt” — roughly “Gen Z’s got this” — posted a statement on Instagram distancing itself from “any form of violence, as well as violent acts by other groups or individuals” who were not part of the demonstrations. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt accused “violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from the immigrant community’’ of hijacking peaceful demonstrations. “The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable,’' Dobrindt told daily paper Bild on Sunday. In Portugal, riot police overnight removed protesters by force from a square in Lisbon following protests for more affordable housing. Thousands of people marched through the city during the day and at the end a few hundred camped out in Rossio, an iconic square in downtown Lisbon. Police intervened early Sunday, removing tents and pushing people away, and a few were detained. Portuguese demonstrators have been protesting for weeks following inspiration from the Spanish movement to call out rising living costs, especially housing costs. Grieshaber reported from Berlin. Helena Alves in Lisbon, Portugal, contributed to this report.

Haley Stevens stuns Democrats by endorsing GOP's Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
articles.description: Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, has stunned party officials by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers.
articles.content: Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, right, and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., attend a service at Perfecting Church, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Jose Juarez)(Jose Juarez/AP Photo/Jose Juarez / FR171038 AP)DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary.“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later Sunday, saying he's focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living.“At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens," he said, adding later: “None of this matters."Michigan Democratic leaders were left shocked. With just less than 48 hours to go before Election Day, a party that had spent months trying to unite behind its Senate nominee was suddenly grappling with an extraordinary defection in one of this year's most important races.Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is facing Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by the retiring Democrat, Gary Peters. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term.Stevens and El-Sayed were originally scheduled to attend church together, along with other Michigan and national Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. Democrats hoped it would be a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds.Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded.Stevens' team resigns as Democrats are stunned by reversalAfter the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and her fiance Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.”Rogers, standing beside her, said he was “honored” by her support.Their appearance came days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed she would vote for her party's nominee. It also led her longtime chief of staff to resign, with a number of staff members expected to follow soon, according to a person familiar with the developments who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters.“We are shocked and heartbroken,” the aide said in a statement.The state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said Stevens' endorsement “shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about.”“We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum," Hertel wrote, and won't let such 11th-hour “distractions” deter the campaign. Hertel later wrote that Stevens "is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future."Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, who supported Stevens in the primary, denounced her endorsement of Rogers.“This is a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens,” Schumer wrote in a social media post.Dingell says she disinvited Stevens after it became ‘distracting’Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church Sunday morning were U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began.Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that.“I'm the one who pulled it, because it had become way too distracting," Dingell said in an interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.”In the August primary, Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighboring Oakland County, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition.Early voting for Tuesday's election has been underway since October 24. As of Friday, more than 1.8 million people had already voted in Michigan.How did we get here?The Democratic primary was among the most bitter this year. Each candidate accused the other of making personal attacks. Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending poured into the race, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s affiliated super PAC, which backed Stevens. El-Sayed took particular offense to an outside group’s ad accusing him of disrespecting women.Although Stevens pledged after the primary to help El-Sayed however she could, the two have not appeared together publicly since a unity breakfast two days after his primary win.Last week Stevens’ fiance told The Detroit News that he would vote for Rogers. Stevens later appeared on CNN to reaffirm her support for El-Sayed but urged his campaign to “shut out the hate and call it out.”But on Friday, after The Associated Press reported on the planned joint appearance, Stevens released a lengthy statement calling on El-Sayed to condemn an ad by an independent left-wing group that linked U.S. support for Israel to high grocery prices.“Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”El-Sayed responded: “So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand.”He made clear the ad was not made by his campaign and said “I do not agree with the contents of that ad.”Trump and Republicans revel in the discordTrump praised Stevens in a Truth Social post, saying she was “a Highly Respected Democrat” and that her support from Black and Jewish voters in Michigan is “virtually unprecedented.”“Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” Trump wrote. “It’s a thing called bravery, and few people have it like just displayed by Congresswoman Haley Stevens!”Appearing with Trump in Iowa for a campaign rally, House Speaker Mike Johnson said that he spoke to Stevens after she endorsed Rogers. Johnson said he “encouraged her to stay safe and keep speaking the truth.”A spokesman for the Republican National Committee, Hunter Lovell, said Democrats who feel abandoned by El-Sayed “have a home” with Rogers.

Related: Haley Stevens endorses Mike Rogers, bucking Abdul El-Sayed Rogers vs. El-Sayed: What to know about US Senate race in Michigan Fact checks, takeaways: Trump downplays gas prices in Michigan His remarks came as part of an 11th hour telephone town hall effort focused on 19 states, including Texas, Alaska, Florida and New Mexico, according to the Republican National Committee. Trump is not expected to campaign again in Michigan before Tuesday’s midterm election, but as he did in an Oct. 25 rally in Port Huron, urged voters here to “pretend” he is on the ballot. “Michigan, you have to go out and vote,” Trump said after vouching for Rogers, gubernatorial nominee John James and Republican candidates for the US House. “If the people that voted for me vote, we have a landslide for Mike, John James, Bill Huizenga, Mike Bouchard and Tom Barrett.” It’s not clear how many voters were on the line for the call. Each is currently held by Republicans but are considered toss-ups and have emerged as some of the most expensive US House races ever. Trump’s appeal to Michigan voters came just days after an appearance from Vice President JD Vance, who stumped in Howell on Tuesday for many of these same candidates — and on many of the same issues. articles.description: Sudan’s power grid nears collapse as drone strikes blamed on RSF target electric stations AP News Sudan files complaints against Ethiopia with UN over deadly drone spree Al Jazeera RSF drone strikes knock out power stations in northern Sudan Sudan Tribune News: Sudan says 70 drone attacks launched from Ethiopia killed, wounded hundreds over eight months Addis Standard Sudan accuses Ethiopia of direct involvement in d
articles.content: CAIRO (AP) — Drone strikes knocked out power substations in two northern Sudanese towns on Sunday, the latest in a week of attacks on electricity stations across army-held areas that Sudan’s government and a rights group blamed on the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The strikes on Al-Dabbah in Northern state and Abu Hamad in River Nile state left both towns without power. The attacks have disrupted electricity and water supplies, halted business activity and forced residents to rely on costly alternatives, driving up prices. The Sudan Doctors Network warned the outages endanger hospitals, dialysis centers and blood banks, and threaten the cold storage needed for medicines and vaccines. Fifteen substations have been targeted since early October, Emergency Lawyers, a Sudanese rights group tracking the attacks, said, leaving the war-torn country’s grid dependent on a handful of plants. In Al-Dabbah, residents woke to an explosion shortly after 4 a.m. Sunday. The town hosts thousands of people, many of whom fled after the RSF seized the city of Al Fasher last year. “We heard a huge explosion that shook the houses, and then the power went out,” said Abbas Wadaa, a resident. When residents went to the substation after sunrise, they said they found it completely burned. The station’s guard, Mohammed al-Nour, was killed, and a large crowd from the city attended his funeral, Wadaa said. The outage has shut down markets, hospitals and bakeries. “We have a generator, but there’s no diesel in the city,” said Seif al-Rawasi, a baker in the city, who said he would eventually have to shut down his business without access to electricity. “We don’t know why the RSF is targeting citizens by destroying power stations,” he added. Farmers face an even bigger threat at the start of the winter growing season because irrigation depends on electricity and there is no diesel in the area to run pumps. In Abu Hamad, a drone strike the same day destroyed the substation and knocked it out of service but caused no casualties, the local security committee said. Emergency Lawyers blamed the RSF for Sunday’s strikes on Al-Dabbah and Abu Hamad. The wave of attacks began late Wednesday, when drones hit the Um Dabakir thermal power station in White Nile state, the country’s largest thermal plant with a capacity of 500 megawatts, according to an employee at the Sudan Electric Holding Company, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media. The attack destroyed four transformers and damaged three generating units, shutting down the station, its director said in a statement. White Nile and North Kordofan states have been cut off from the grid, and the damage will be felt for months, the regional network director said. Early on Friday, a drone carrying four missiles destroyed the transformers at Shendi’s main substation, the local security committee said. The attack also hit a reserve depot and an army air defense hangar, wounding a soldier. The Merowe Dam, with a capacity of 1,250 megawatts, is now the last major source of electricity in the country, providing more than 70% of Sudan’s electricity, according to the Electricity Holding Company employee. The country’s other hydroelectric dams produce no more than 100 megawatts combined, the employee said. Even before the latest attacks, production had fallen from 4,400 megawatts before the war to 1,100. Many Sudanese who can afford it have turned to solar panels to cope with the blackout, but a typical household system costs nearly $5,000, far beyond the reach of most families, a solar business owner in Khartoum told The Associated Press earlier this year. Sudan’s Foreign Ministry said Saturday the drones were supplied by the United Arab Emirates and launched from Ethiopia. The UAE has repeatedly denied arming the RSF. The RSF did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The war has killed at least 59,000 people, though aid groups warn that the number could be much higher. The war has also displaced some 13 million people and pushed parts of the country into famine. ___ Abdallah reported from Shendi, Sudan

articles.title: Medicare drug plans are hiking premiums while Trump claims victory on medicine prices
articles.description: Millions of Medicare enrollees who buy stand-alone prescription drug plans will see their average monthly premiums rise by 50% in 2027, a new analysis finds. But enrollees can avoid the average increase — from $34 a month to $51 — by switching to lower-cost plans during the program’s open enrollment period, which runs through Dec. […]
articles.content: (Eric Harkleroad/KFF Health News)Millions of Medicare enrollees who buy stand-alone prescription drug plans will see their average monthly premiums rise by 50% in 2027, a new analysis finds. But enrollees can avoid the average increase — from $34 a month to $51 — by switching to lower-cost plans during the program’s open enrollment period, which runs through Dec. 7. Robert Travis Scott of Abingdon, Virginia, did just that in late October after he received a notice that his AARP-UnitedHealthcare Medicare drug plan premium would be increasing from $39.60 a month in 2026 to $121.90 in 2027. With just a little work checking prices online, Scott found a Humana plan for $19.30 with similar benefits. “Yes, I am quite happy about that,” he said of the new plan he just found. He said he was stunned his existing plan was going up so much and worried that other seniors won’t shop for plans to save money. He estimates he saved himself about $1,000 for next year. “With some plans increasing premiums substantially, the stakes are higher this year for people with Medicare stand-alone drug coverage if they sit on the sidelines during open enrollment,” said Juliette Cubanski, a vice president and the director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, which conducted the analysis. KFF is a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. Rising drug costs are among the litany of affordability issues angering voters ahead of November’s midterm election. President Donald Trump, whose approval rating in some polls has dipped to the lowest level of his two terms in office, claims his administration has succeeded in negotiating lower prices from drug manufacturers. “What we’re doing great with is pharmaceuticals, hundreds of billions,” Trump said at a campaign rally in Ohio on Oct. 28, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms. “You should win just on this, everybody running. We have the lowest drug prices anywhere in the world. We went from the highest drug prices, we now have the lowest drug prices, favored nations, anywhere in the world.” How much people actually pay for drugs varies widely, depending on what medicines individual patients need and their insurance coverage. Medicare beneficiaries who get their drug coverage as part of private Medicare Advantage plans, which replace traditional Medicare coverage, will see much lower premium increases. The KFF analysis found these enrollees will pay an average of $9 for drugs as part of their overall monthly premium in 2027, or an increase of less than $2 per month. More than half of Medicare beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Advantage health plans, which usually include a drug benefit, instead of the traditional program. Nearly 25 million people are enrolled in Medicare stand-alone prescription drug plans, according to KFF. About 31 million get drug coverage through Medicare Advantage plans. Premiums are just part of the higher costs Medicare enrollees are facing. Most enrollees who buy a stand-alone drug plan or get drug benefits through Medicare Advantage plans will also have an annual deductible for drug coverage in 2027. The average deductible in 2027 will be $643 for stand-alone plans, according to the KFF analysis, up from $540 in 2026. Drug deductibles will average $489 for those with Medicare Advantage plans, up from $360 in 2026. In addition, most Medicare enrollees with drug coverage next year will have to pay coinsurance rather than copayments, the KFF analysis found. That can mean less predictable out-of-pocket costs because coinsurance requires paying a percentage of the cost of a drug, not a fixed amount. One possible cause of the projected premium hikes is the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ decision in July to end early a three-year pilot program designed to keep down stand-alone premiums. The program paid subsidies to stand-alone plans in 2025 and 2026. KFF said CMS’ decision to end that subsidy program after only two years could cause stand-alone premiums to rise in 2027. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz has called the subsidy program an insurance industry bailout. KFF noted its analysis differs from CMS’ projection for a $1 increase in the national average premium, from $35 to $36, based on September 2026 enrollment. It said that CMS did not explain its calculation methods and that it’s possible CMS assumed people would switch to lower-cost plans. CMS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the KFF findings. About 10.4 million Medicare enrollees, or 76% of enrollees in stand-alone drug plans who don’t get low-income subsidies, will pay a higher monthly premium in 2027 if they stick with the same plan, KFF found. This includes 4.1 million enrollees who are currently in a zero-premium plan. They’ll automatically pay more in 2027, because there will be no zero-premium plans available, the KFF analysis found. KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism.
