articles.title: Haley Stevens endorses Mike Rogers, bucking Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race
articles.description: US Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican US Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday amid tensions with Democratic primary rival Abdul El-Sayed.
articles.content: Democratic US Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers for US Senate and joined him at a church Detroit The endorsement came as Democrats prepared a ‘unity rally’ for Abdul El-Sayed, who beat Stevens in the primary El-Sayed and Rogers are locked in a tight battle for Michigan’s open US Senate seat DETROIT — Democratic US Rep. Haley Stevens on Sunday endorsed Republican Mike Rogers for US Senate, bucking former primary rival Abdul El-Sayed just two days before the Nov. 3 election. “Abdul made very clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn’t need me there, that he didn’t want me there, and at some point, you got to look at who’s standing for country,” Stevens said after joining Rogers at Perfecting Church in Detroit. “We have to stand with country. We can’t stand with hate,” she added, referencing the running feud she has had with El-Sayed over US support for the Israeli government. More fact checks: Rogers backed abortion bans, says he won’t undo Michigan rights Mike Rogers claims Abdul El-Sayed wants an ‘energy tax’ Mike Rogers faces voter suppression claims over Detroit comments Rogers called Stevens’ decision “courage in politics,” characterizing the unlikely political pairing as “a statement about standing together against hate and the future of this state and this country than it is anything else.” “Candidly, I’m glad I’m not running against Haley Stevens today,” he told reporters during a Sunday press conference. Stevens’ endorsement came as other Democrats were headed to a separate church event in Detroit in an attempt to present a united front behind El-Sayed in a race that could decide control of the U.S. Senate. Speaking to reporters after the event, El-Sayed said he is focused on fighting for the needs of other Michiganders — not Stevens, who he said he doesn’t think about much. “If you’re somebody who believes that we should stand up to hate, and you have watched this last campaign, I think we probably would not want to support Mike Rogers and Donald Trump and JD Vance,” he said. Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks with reporters before a Souls to the Polls campaign event at Northend Church of God in Christ, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) Several fellow Democrats criticized Stevens, including state party Chair Curtis Hertel. He said her decision to campaign with Rogers “shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about. Donate “We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us,” Hertel added. In a social media post, Hertel said “Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.” By Sunday night, her photo had been removed from a list of elected officials on the party’s website. Stevens congressional chief of staff Justin German immediately resigned and said “many” other employees in her office had as well. In a statement, he encouraged Michiganders to vote for El-Sayed and “stand up for the America we all believe in.” But Republicans like former national and Michigan GOP Chair Ronna McDaniel praised Stevens for “putting our state before party.” “It takes courage to do this and while some will attack you, just know this is exactly what we need more of in this country,” McDaniel said on social media. On social media, Trump praised Stevens for saying “what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan.” How we got here Stevens, who lost in the primary to El-Sayed, was initially set to join El-Sayed and US Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina at the “unity” event. Those plans unraveled after a dispute over Israel and an outside group’s campaign advertisement escalated into a public exchange of criticism between the rivals. Debbie Dingell, the Michigan representative who helped organize the planned joint appearance in hopes of bringing together Democrats in the final days before Tuesday’s vote, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that. “I’m the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting,” Dingell told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. “This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank.” “The bishop was getting upset, because this is a real church service,” Dingell added. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., left, her fiance Jason Turkish, right, stand with Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, second left, and his wife Kristi Rogers during a church service at Perfecting Church, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Jose Juarez) The latest and late-stage infighting comes as Democrats look to drive turnout among Black and Jewish voters in key strongholds. El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is in a tight race with Mike Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by Democrat Gary Peters, who is retiring. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Republican President Donald Trump’s second term. Dingell and other Democrats insist the party is united behind El-Sayed, who would be the country’s first Muslim senator if elected. Early voting has been underway since Oct. 24, before the latest tensions erupted. But the renewed bickering has complicated Democrats’ efforts to deliver a unified closing message in crucial areas such as Detroit, where turnout could prove decisive. “All you guys want to talk about was Abdul and Haley and it really needs to be about what the issues are that people should be voting about on Tuesday,” Dingell said. She added about El-Sayed’s Republican opponent: “Mike Rogers loved every minute of it.” The tensions carry particular significance in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighboring Oakland County. Stevens defeated El-Sayed in both counties in the August primary, drawing support from Black and Jewish voters who are important parts of the Democratic coalition. Throughout the primary cycle, Stevens promised to endorse the Democratic nominee and did so following her loss to El-Sayed. Earlier this week, she told CNN she would still vote for El-Sayed after her fiance Jason Turkish, a Jewish Democrat and civil rights attorney, said he planned to vote for Rogers in the general election. Following that announcement, El-Sayed told reporters “there are always going to be some folks who have different opinions, and they’re welcome to that.” “If folks see another issue that is more important to them and decide that their disagreement with me on that is bigger than their disagreement with me on all these other things, that is their choice,” he said.

articles.description: The cryptocurrency exchange said it's now covered 95% of the stolen assets.
articles.content: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance announced early on Sunday that it would begin allowing withdrawals in a phased process. The company froze all deposits and withdrawals after hackers stole $6.3 billion worth of crypto from Binance wallets. In its latest update, Binance said it has now covered 95% of the stolen assets, and it’s still working to buy the “remaining affected assets,” which are “less liquid in the market and take longer time to source at the required scale.” “Our commitment remains unchanged: Binance will bear the financial impact of the stolen funds,” the company added. “These losses will not be passed on to users.” As for the withdrawal freeze, Binance said it did not make the decision lightly, as it understands “how important reliable access to withdrawals is for our users.” Nonetheless, the company said this was a necessary “precaution while our teams worked to contain the incident loss, assess its impact, restore affected services, and complete security checks.” Binance will resume supporting withdrawals in phases, depending on network and asset type. As of Sunday morning, the company’s network status page showed a mix of normal, partially suspended, and fully suspended statuses — for example, Bitcoin withdrawals and deposits are still listed as partially suspended, while Ethereum deposits are normal and withdrawals are partially suspended. The company also said users should expect “temporary delays or longer processing times due to traffic volume.” “Resuming withdrawals is a major milestone, but our work continues,” Binance said. “We will continue strengthening our safeguards, completing the recovery process, and providing updates as progress continues.” Binance subsequently shared that between 6am and 3:30pm Coordinated Universal Time, it processed $4.6 billion in withdrawals and $1.0 billion in deposits, for a net outflow of $3.6 billion — 2.1% of its total assets under management. The company also said it will publish a more in-depth incident report when its investigation is complete. Binance previously blamed North Korea hackers for the breach. On Saturday, the FBI said that a North Korean group known as TraderTraitor was responsible, and that the group was converting the assets primarily into Ethereum, with further laundering likely. articles.description: Civilians in Ukraine’s Kherson prepare for the return of war as localized ceasefire ends AP News A brief ceasefire opens a perilous escape window from Kherson’s riverside kill zone AP News ‘We Are Coming From Hell’: A Ukrainian City’s Evacuees Tell Survival Stories The New York Times Reunited after 1,711 days: Oleshky evacuees return to Ukraine under Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire CNN Russian Offensive Campaign Ass
articles.content: KHERSON, Ukraine (AP) — Civilians in Ukraine’s southeastern Kherson region prepared Sunday for the end of a localized ceasefire that has marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began nearly five years ago. The White House said that U.S. first lady Melania Trump helped to broker the limited truce, which began early Tuesday and is expected to end Sunday evening. The pause in hostilities allowed besieged residents in the front-line city of Oleshky to be evacuated in a rare joint operation that ended Saturday. “The ceasefire across Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack,” Trump said on social media. “Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace.” An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of evacuating to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. For the safety of those who have stayed, exact numbers weren’t released after the evacuation. At the Ukrainian border Saturday, family members waited for a glimpse of their loved ones, while residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and flashlights to greet the humanitarian convoy. But Moscow and Kyiv have continued aerial strikes elsewhere, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying Sunday that Russia continues to target Ukraine’s energy systems before winter. Hundreds of thousands of families were left without power overnight as Moscow sought to exploit Ukraine’s shortage of air defenses, Zelenskyy said in a post on social media. “The intensity of the strikes is extremely high, and the Russians are trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors,” he said in a post on X. Residents in the Ukrainian city of Kherson remained calm Sunday, despite knowing that the quiet of the localized ceasefire would soon end. “Don’t be afraid, keep holding on,” Oleksandr Knyha, head of the Mykola Kulish Kherson Regional Academic Music and Drama Theater, told the audience as he opened a concert. The theater performs every Saturday and Sunday. This weekend’s shows fell during the ceasefire, but the company plans to perform next weekend as usual, even as local officials warn that Russian forces have brought in more weapons and personnel and some residents expect shelling to intensify. “Of course, we want peace to finally come,” Knyha said. But “we’ve been working on the front line for four years,” he added, referring to Kherson itself, and the theater has never canceled a performance. “Whatever happens, the show is not canceled,” he said. The company now performs in a basement and is equipping an additional bomb shelter. About 100 of the theater’s 120 staff members work in Kherson, and none has evacuated. Costume maker Alla Vasylenko, 58, said that the silence of the brief truce still frightens her. “Nothing will change,” she said. “Everything will go back to how it was before the ceasefire, because believing the Russians means not believing yourself.” “I have 10 dogs, so I can’t leave,” she said. “They urge us to leave, but you need somewhere to go and the means to get there.” The trip alone would cost 30,000 to 50,000 hryvnias ($650 to $1,080), a significant sum for her, she said. “Until we liberate the left bank, we have no certainty this will end,” Vasylenko said, referring to the Russia-occupied part of the region. For many in Kherson, a city that itself lived through Russian occupation, that belief is the reason they stay. Knyha is from Oleshky, on the occupied left bank, and used to commute from there to work in Kherson. He hasn’t given up hope of returning home. “That’s also what keeps me here,” he said. On the last day of the ceasefire, the theater staged a concert built around a “musical map of Ukraine,” with songs from the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014, to the Carpathian mountains in Ukraine’s southwest. “This is also our job — to unite people and give them hope,” Knyha said. Elsewhere, a Russian attack killed three people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Ukrainian region of Vinnytsia when a drone hit the grounds of a vocational school, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. Four others were wounded, including two 5-year-old girls and a 16-year-old boy. Russian drone attacks also continued to target Ukraine’s Kyiv region for a second consecutive day, wounding a woman and damaging homes, energy infrastructure and a retail establishment, regional authorities said. In its daily report Sunday, Ukraine’s air force said that Moscow’s forces attacked Ukraine with 433 drones overnight, of which 371 were destroyed or suppressed. Elsewhere, more than 100 Ukrainian drones were shot down over the skies of Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region east of Moscow, local Gov. Gleb Nikitin said Sunday. Nikitin said an industrial building in the town of Kstovo had sustained “significant damage,” but didn’t give further details. Russian media outlets later reported that the attack sparked a blaze at the Kstovo oil refinery, sharing images of black plumes of smoke over the horizon. Local officials later placed limits on gasoline sales in the region after lines appeared at gas stations, Russian media outlets reported, citing Nizhny Novgorod’s regional government. Diesel sales weren’t affected, they said. Zelenskyy said Sunday that Kyiv had also struck a factory used to make missile components and air defense facilities inside Russia’s southern Rostov region. “We are justly defending ourselves against Russian aggression and doing everything to reduce Russia’s capability to continue it,” Zelenskyy wrote. Katie Marie Davies contributed to this report from Manchester, England. Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

Drummond Island, off Michigan's Upper Peninsula, chases 100% voter turnout
articles.description: Residents on this remote island say they're tired of national issues — but they'll vote on a school millage and local government races.
articles.content: Drummond Island, just to the eat of Michigan's Upper Peninsula, has a limestone bedrock lakeshore.(Jesse M. Lincoln / MSU Extension Michigan Natural Features Inventory)History tells us 2 in 5 Michiganders will not vote in this year’s midterm elections. But one island off the eastern tip of the Upper Peninsula is hoping to change that.Going to the polls in Drummond Island Township isn’t easy. There’s only one precinct for its 134 square miles. And that’s just for Election Day. Early in-person voting isn’t on the island. It’s in Kincheloe, on the Upper Peninsula mainland.“That is a 50-mile one-way trip off the island,” Drummond Island Township Supervisor Krystal Truax said. "So, you have the ferry fare plus the time, plus the hour there, then you vote, then the hour back, [then] back on to the ferry.”A little over a thousand registered voters live on the island. They usually beat statewide turnout. In the 2024 presidential election, 74% of residents showed up. During the 2022 midterms, 63% came out.This year, Truax is joining an effort to get everyone out to the polls — all 1,116 of them.“My thought is that if we can do it, anyone can do it, because we have so many real barriers keeping us away from early voting, from voting in person,” she said.The campaign started with technology entrepreneur Bob Chunn, who moved to the island with his wife during the COVID-19 pandemic.Chunn got involved in politics because he felt discouraged after the 2016 election. Chunn created a nonprofit to turn out the vote by providing voters with information. Now, he’s testing a new strategy on the island.“It’s kind of an experiment to see how high you can push the envelope. The bar is pretty darn low in my view,” he said.The plan involves sending reminders, knocking on doors, and helping organize rides to the polls.Chunn said Drummond Island is a tightknit community. He's finding people who could personally reach out to folks who haven't voted in recent years.When he meets people who feel turned off by politics, Chunn focuses on what’s happening locally. For example, he’s promoted a school millage on the ballot.“Immediately, when people start talking about Washington, Lansing, they don’t like politicians, I’m saying skip all that. Don’t vote for any of it. But vote for the millage, the schools,” Chunn said.That’s the message Chunn and his co-organizers spread this month at a town hall event. There, resident Tom Salwoski volunteered to share his reason for staying home in past elections.Salwoski felt like his vote didn’t matter. Especially amid the slew of negative ads and politicians talking about issues far from home.“Everything feels national. Even the ads that are local to Michigan, those are all about Trump or the Republican party,” Salwoski said. “They’re kind of all lumped into the national with everything. And so, that’s another turn off.”But hearing about the millages and local races that are also on the ballot changed his mind. He said he hadn’t learned too much about those in the past.Knowing that he could be the deciding factor for a local millage or township race resonated with him.“It’s all stuff that I heard about but just never understood it. So now that I understand a little bit more, I feel more comfortable about going down the ballot and learning a little bit more, which I wasn’t really open to before,” Salwoski said.As the adage goes, all politics is local. With each Drummond Island resident the volunteers reach with that message, the hope is that they tick up voter turnout and set an example for the rest of the state.One local issue at a time.

What is Sharia law, and why is it so controversial in the United States?
articles.description: Asma Uddin, Michigan State University; Institute for Humane Studies At a campaign rally, in Port Huron, Michigan, on Oct. 25, 2026, President Donald Trump accused U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of being a “jihadist” who wants to impose Sharia law – Islamic law – in the United States. His comments reflect a broader pattern among […]
articles.content: For Muslims, Sharia refers to the divinely guided principles of living a moral life. sean zheng lim/iStock via Getty Images Plus Asma Uddin, Michigan State University; Institute for Humane Studies At a campaign rally, in Port Huron, Michigan, on Oct. 25, 2026, President Donald Trump accused U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of being a “jihadist” who wants to impose Sharia law – Islamic law – in the United States. His comments reflect a broader pattern among Republican politicians of portraying Sharia as a threat to the American legal system. In March 2026, Texas legislators launched the Sharia Free Texas Caucus, a group dedicated to preventing what its members describe as the spread of Islamic law in Texas. Its founder, state Rep. Brent Money, has characterized Sharia as “an entire civilizational legal structure” that threatens American law and institutions. That same month, nearly 95% of Texas Republican primary voters backed a nonbinding proposition declaring that “Texas should prohibit Sharia Law.” The movement extends beyond Texas. In Congress, the Sharia Free America Caucus, established in December 2025, grew to 68 Republican lawmakers from 25 states in just six months. These efforts reflect a long-standing claim, frequently invoked by anti-Sharia activists, that Muslims are seeking to establish a parallel legal system that will eventually replace American law. But this rhetoric raises a more basic question: What exactly is Sharia, and what does it actually mean for Muslims to follow it while living in the United States? I am a law professor who studies religious liberty. My 2019 book, “When Islam Is Not a Religion,” examined how ordinary Muslim religious practices come to be treated as political threats, and I recently documented that pattern in Texas. The Sharia controversy shows how this happens. Sharia is not a single legal code In Arabic, “sharia” means a path or way, literally “the path to a watering place.” For Muslims, it refers to the divinely ordained way of living a moral and religious life, guided by the Quran and the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad. Sharia guides Muslims how to pray, when to fast, what to eat and how much to give to charity. It also addresses marriage and divorce. These rules span what Americans would sort into law, ethics, manners and worship, as law professor and an authority on Islamic law Asifa Quraishi-Landes has explained. This distinction matters because Americans often think of law as something established and enforced by the state. Sharia is broader than that. A Muslim who avoids pork or prays five times a day may see each practice as part of following Sharia, but neither requires a separate legal court or government enforcement. Rules governing marriage, divorce and inheritance, by contrast, may have legal consequences, though how they are interpreted and applied varies across Islamic traditions. Indeed, as Quraishi-Landes notes, Sharia itself obliges Muslims to follow the law of the land wherever they live. Who decides what Sharia requires? Muslims do not all agree on how Sharia should be interpreted. They distinguish between Sharia, which they regard as the divine ideal, and “fiqh,” the human effort to understand and apply it. In other words, Muslims believe Sharia comes from God, but people must figure out what it requires in practice. Because people can disagree, interpretations can differ and change over time. For Muslims, Sharia is an expression of divine guidance. Bay Ismoyo/AFP via Getty Images Sunni Islam’s four major schools and Shiite Islam’s legal traditions sometimes reach different conclusions about matters such as marriage, divorce and financial transactions. For example, scholars differ on whether Muslims can take out conventional mortgages to buy homes, given Islamic prohibitions on interest, and on the conditions under which a marriage can be dissolved. They continue to debate newer questions, too, such as whether organ donation is permissible or how modern banking can comply with Islamic principles. No single institution speaks for all Muslims. Yet political debates often treat Sharia as a fixed rule book, when much of the Islamic legal tradition consists of ongoing disagreements about what its rules mean and how they should apply. How does Sharia work in the US? Muslims are subject to the same laws as everyone else in the United States. Their religious commitments may guide personal decisions about marriage, divorce, finances and everyday conduct, but Sharia has no independent legal authority. Muslims can follow religious rules voluntarily, but those rules cannot override American law. This is not unique to Islam. Religious communities across the country have long used their own procedures to resolve disputes. For example, many Orthodox Jewish couples sign prenuptial agreements committing them to appear before a Jewish religious court, known as a beth din, if their marriage breaks down. The court can then help facilitate a religious divorce, including addressing situations in which a husband refuses to grant his wife a religious divorce. Christian organizations likewise offer biblical mediation and arbitration to resolve conflicts according to religious principles. Muslims can similarly turn to religious scholars or mediators for guidance on family or financial disputes. These arrangements are generally voluntary, and any legally enforceable agreement must comply with American law. A religious ruling does not become binding simply because a religious authority issues it. Like other religious communities, Muslims may organize aspects of their personal lives around their faith, but they do so within the framework of American law. Can American courts enforce Sharia? Critics often claim Sharia is gaining a foothold in the courts. The concern usually arises when Muslims ask a court to recognize a religious contract or arbitration. Consider an Islamic marriage contract promising the wife a marriage gift, known as “mahr,” some or all of which may be payable if the couple divorces. A court asked to enforce it does not decide what Islamic theology requires. It asks whether the agreement meets ordinary contract law. In 2020, a Maryland appeals court held that a “mahr” could be enforced only under the same secular standards that apply to any agreement between spouses. In other words, the court’s job is to determine whether the couple’s agreement is legally enforceable, just as it would with any other contract. It is not enforcing Islamic religious law. Courts may apply what the Supreme Court calls “neutral principles of law.” That simply means applying ordinary legal rules without deciding religious questions. A judge can determine whether two people entered into a valid contract, for example, but cannot decide which interpretation of Islam is religiously correct. As law professor Haider Ala Hamoudi has observed, courts can enforce a “mahr” agreement precisely because doing so does not require them to interpret Islamic law. Arbitration works the same way. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has called Islamic panels “Sharia tribunals masquerading as legal courts.” Yet the Beth Din of America also structures its proceedings so civil courts can enforce its rulings, as do Christian arbitrators. Courts can enforce voluntary arbitration awards and can also vacate them for fraud or overreach. For example, suppose a Muslim couple voluntarily agree to have a religious arbitrator resolve a financial dispute. If the arbitrator orders one spouse to pay the other US$10,000, a court may enforce that decision just as it would any other arbitration award. But if one spouse was coerced into participating or the arbitrator exceeded the authority the couple had agreed to give them, a court could set the decision aside. A religious arbitrator cannot override a statute or the Constitution. Why is Sharia so controversial? Protesters in Toronto, Canada, call for an end to Sharia law in Iran, on Sept. 20, 2018. Creative Touch Imaging Ltd./NurPhoto via Getty Images Some concerns stem from how certain governments enforce Islamic law. In Iran, U.N. investigators have documented escalating violence against women accused of violating hijab rules. In Afghanistan, the Taliban have issued more than 100 decrees targeting women and girls. These policies raise serious questions about religious coercion, gender equality and freedom of conscience. Muslim scholars and reformers have long debated those questions themselves. One example is Musawah, an international movement founded in Malaysia in 2009 that advocates equality and justice in Muslim family laws. Working with scholars and activists across the world, it argues that Islamic teachings can support women’s rights and challenges discriminatory interpretations of religious law. American debates often collapse these issues into one question: whether Sharia itself is compatible with American law. That framing obscures a crucial distinction. A government imposing religious rules on unwilling citizens is doing something fundamentally different from an individual choosing to follow them. A Muslim woman who wears a hijab is not asking the government to mandate religious dress. The American campaign against Sharia Between 2010 and 2012, lawmakers in at least 32 states introduced bills to keep courts from applying Sharia or foreign law. In 2010, Oklahoma voters approved a constitutional amendment barring courts from considering Sharia. A federal appeals court upheld an injunction against the amendment, finding that it likely violated the First Amendment’s protection of religious freedom by singling out Islam for unfavorable treatment. In 2013, a federal judge struck it down permanently. Other states adopted broader bans on the use of foreign law. Supporters say these measures protect women’s rights. Critics argue that they address a problem American law already guards against: Courts cannot enforce agreements that violate fundamental legal protections. For example, a court can reject an agreement obtained through coercion or fraud, or one that violates a person’s constitutional rights or other applicable laws. Those protections apply regardless of whether an agreement is based on religious principles. The effort has now reached Congress: In June 2026, U.S. Rep. Keith Self of Texas introduced a bill to bar federal courts from enforcing foreign or religious laws that conflict with the Constitution. But courts already cannot enforce agreements that violate the Constitution or other applicable laws. The proposed restriction thus raises a basic question: What additional protection would it provide? The central point is that American law already provides safeguards against religious rules being imposed through the courts. Muslims, like members of other faiths, can organize their personal lives around their religious beliefs. But those beliefs do not carry independent legal authority, and courts cannot enforce them in ways that violate applicable American law. The debate over Sharia is not just about religious law. It is also about whether Americans are willing to extend the same understanding of religious freedom to Muslims that they extend to other faiths. Asma Uddin, Assistant Professor of Law, Michigan State University; Institute for Humane Studies. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. articles.title: Rioters clash with police as France faces third week of violent protests
articles.content: Demonstrations also taking place in Germany, where officers fire teargas to disperse crowds as evening falls Clashes erupted in Paris, Marseille and other cities on Saturday after tens of thousands of demonstrators, some in Halloween fancy dress, marched across France in a third wave of protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services. The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said about 150 planned demonstrations around the country had passed off peacefully, but police had encountered an “extraordinary” level of violence from some rioters as the rallies ended. One riot police officer had been hit by a molotov cocktail in Paris, he said, describing the incident as an “attempted murder”. “We are fully prepared for those looking for confrontation tonight,” he added. About 320,000 people – down from an estimated 410,000 last weekend – took part in rallies around the country, the interior ministry said, including 70,000 in Paris who marched along boulevards on the south-eastern outskirts, avoiding the city centre. As evening approached and the largely peaceful demonstrations came to an end, police in several cities fired teargas and stun grenades to disperse crowds joined – as on the previous Saturday – by groups of masked rioters. The interior ministry said late Saturday that police had arrested 565 people across the country. Four police officers and one gendarme were injured in Paris. Nuñez said earlier this week that 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the protests’ sidelines, warning that Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day. The Paris protesters set off peacefully from the Porte de Bagnolet near the ring road, holding placards with slogans including “No need for teargas to make our future look bleak” and “Disguised as an angry citizen for Halloween”, as a helicopter flew overhead On and around its destination, the Porte de Charenton, dozens of masked people dressed in black used hammers to pry up paving stones and hurl them at police, and at least one incendiary device was thrown at security forces. Police responded with teargas and baton charges. “A hardcore of several hundred rioters” had attacked police with projectiles, the Paris police prefecture said. Officers had “manoeuvred to restore public order”, it added. In Lyon protesters threw projectiles at police, prompting officers to fire teargas, and in Toulouse police used water cannon against an unauthorised protest that drew several thousand people, mostly young demonstrators. The marches brought together school students, who have been calling for better conditions for a month, trade unions and gilets jaune (yellow vests) protesters united in anger at the cost of living, widening inequalities and Emmanuel Macron’s government. “The French economy is doing badly no matter what happens, because today we’re being run by a group of incompetents who juggle billions while families are struggling with a few cents,” said one protester on the Paris march, Jérôme Rodrigues. “That’s why we’re here, to keep shouting our demands louder and louder.” A protester in Nantes, Camille Guérin, said: “We say no to the cost of living, no to the far right, yes to high school students’ demands, yes to giving citizens a voice.” Saturday’s rallies came two weeks after widespread street violence and looting rocked numerous French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October that became one of the worst days of civil unrest in the country’s recent history. Student protesters vowed to stage new high school and university blockades on Tuesday and Thursday. “Then we will join the 5 November demonstration called by workers and trade unions,” said Sabrine Kharbach of the Union Étudiante, a student organisation. Protests also took place elsewhere in Europe. In Germany, police fired water cannon to disperse protesters who hurled firework and other projectiles at the end of youth-led protests organised by a group called “Gen Z regelt!” (Gen Z will sort this). Thousands of police were deployed across the country, with tensions rising as evening fell after mostly peaceful demonstrations for “for education, health, the climate and an affordable life” in dozens of cities. In Frankfurt, Germany’s financial hub, at least two stores were looted as protests turned violent, with several more damaged and police trying to gain control of the situation, according to a Reuters witness. A march was also temporarily halted in the city after protesters set off fireworks. In the western city of Cologne, police fired water cannon to disperse a crowd after saying protesters had targeted officers with fireworks. In Berlin, protesters hurled bottles and eggs while protesters set barricades ablaze in Hamburg, and police were using pepper spray on demonstrators in some places, the newspaper Bild reported. Fresh anti-government demonstrations also occurred in Albania’s capital, with protesters renewing their demands that prime minister Edi Rama resign. Saturday’s demonstration began peacefully under rain outside the education ministry in Tirana, before dozens of masked youths started throwing paving stones and firebombs at police and set fire to rubbish bins. Police were also on alert in Barcelona after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings, and in Italy after recent clashes with protesters in Milan, Turin and Bologna.

Voters on Saturday crossed the high-water mark of 52.7 million early votes cast, surpassing the midterm record set in 2022, […]
articles.content: King County, Washington, election workers dump out a bin full of ballots from a local drop box to sort ahead of the midterm election on Oct. 29, 2026, in Renton, Washington. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)WASHINGTON — When the polls close Tuesday night, the 2026 U.S. election will go down as one of history’s most expensive and extraordinarily ugly midterms — galvanizing record-breaking early voter turnout among a deeply divided electorate. Voters on Saturday crossed the high-water mark of 52.7 million early votes cast, surpassing the midterm record set in 2022, though analysts were reluctant to translate it into a Democratic wave on the way. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump’s Department of Justice continued to run into a firewall of federal judges, losing its previous cases to take over mail-in balloting and obtain state voter rolls in advance of the midterms. The Trump DOJ actions nonetheless rattled state officials who hold the constitutional responsibility to conduct their elections. “My hope is that this trend will continue and that our worst-case scenarios don’t come to fruition,” former Kentucky Secretary of State Trey Grayson told States Newsroom. A federal appeals court on Friday denied Trump’s efforts to force state officials to quarantine up to 20,000 voter ballots. The department continues to pursue its preemptive lawsuit against Alaska’s U.S. Senate race results, depending on who wins. When asked by reporters Tuesday if he’ll accept a Democratic victory, Trump said, “I will, if they’re honest elections,” refusing to rule out federal interference feared by Democratic critics. President Donald Trump gestures to the crowd at a rally in Dalton, Georgia, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder) Trump insisted in September that his supporters “pretend” he is on the ballot, as his base has turned out in higher numbers during presidential elections to vote for him. “When I’m on the ballot, we kill everybody,” he said at his midterm convention in Texas. He also promised a $5,000 “Trump dividend” to voters if Republicans retained congressional majorities. With GOP control of the House and Senate during the last two years of the Trump presidency in play, campaigns are on track to shell out $11.6 billion on ads, according to the firm AdImpact. The hard-fought Ohio and Texas Senate races led the way in spending. Democrats need to net four seats to control the Senate, while Republicans hold a narrow majority in the House. Campaign advertising hit a low point when Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy aired a $4 million ad in which the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, called Acton “a liar.” The woman, Donna Arthur, has not been in communication with her daughter since the late 1970s, when court records show she lost custody and fled the state with her husband, Acton’s stepfather, after he was indicted for raping Acton. Ramaswamy’s campaign pulled the ad Friday, roughly 10 days after it began to circulate. The ad drew outcry including from outgoing Republican Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, though both Trump and Vice President JD Vance defended it. Voters feel punished by cost of living While ugliness punctuated the campaign season, poll after poll revealed the cost of living remains the top motivator for voters — including fuel prices and the cost of food and everyday goods that have been driven up by Trump’s war with Iran and an erratic tariff policy. Indiana fuel prices spike again on Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle) “It ranks as one of the most important issues for over 80% of voters, and the majority of the electorate disapproves of Trump’s handling, not just of the economy in general, but of cost of living,” economist and former Biden White House economic adviser Jared Bernstein said Tuesday, during a virtual press briefing organized by the Democrat-aligned advocacy group Defend America Action. The GOP also risks losing Latino support on account of the administration’s dragnet immigration enforcement tactics that have targeted legal immigrants, as well as U.S. citizens, and have ended in injury or even death on multiple occasions. María Isabel Di Franco Quiñonez of Equis, a Latino-focused research firm, surveyed 900 Latino voters across seven battleground states and found sinking support for and trust in Republicans. “The clearest finding was that voters want both responsible enforcement and generosity towards immigrants,” she said. “They want a controlled border, enforcement focused on criminals and a pathway to legalization.” Trump ratings Trump’s sagging approval ratings have dogged Republican midterm candidates, giving a major boost to Democrats’ chances of flipping the House — a tried and true pattern for midterm elections — and increasing the competitiveness of several U.S. Senate races. “Given that the president’s not on the ballot, (voters) have no other place to take out their frustration or disappointment or anger, aside from candidates of the president’s party,” said David Dulio, a distinguished professor of political science at Oakland University in Michigan. The state is the site of one of the nation’s most vitriolic U.S. Senate races, between Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and former Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers. U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks to Democratic supporters at a unity rally held at Renaissance High School in Detroit on Aug. 7, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) Democrats are reaching for command of the upper chamber, and if the final prognosticators and polls are correct, they could stand a chance in Republican strongholds. Major forecasts and pollsters more strongly favor Democrats to take the House, though some experts observe that years of gerrymandering, including Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting, combined with entrenched polarization could stunt the crest of a so-called blue wave. Several Republican-led state legislatures, including those in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Tennessee and Texas, split majority Black voter districts after a U.S. Supreme Court decision last year struck down protections that were enshrined in the Voting Rights Act. “I hesitate to say that Republicans are going to lose control of both houses, or Trump is going to be totally hamstrung by this blue wave. The polling has been so shaky in prior election cycles,” said Rob Glover, associate professor of political science at the University of Maine, where longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins is fighting to keep her seat against Democratic challenger Troy Jackson. “But if I was a Republican operative or strategist, I would be concerned,” he said. Senate races As of Friday, The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, a nonpartisan forecaster, rated Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas as toss-up U.S. Senate races. The University of Virginia’s Sabato’s Crystal Ball categorized Alaska as a possible flip. Inside Elections, another nonpartisan forecaster, projected Thursday that Democrats would gain enough seats to reach at least a 50-50 split Senate, ranking Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas as tilting blue. Pollsters have also found Democratic rumblings in time-tested Republican bastions. Wednesday’s New York Times/Siena poll found South Carolina voters, surveyed between Oct. 19 and Oct. 26, evenly split between Republican nominee Darline Graham, who is running to fill the seat of her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham, and her Democratic challenger Annie Andrews, a pediatrician. Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., speaks at a meeting of the Senate Judiciary Committee on Thursday, July 23, 2026. (Screenshot from committee webcast) A survey of Kansas voters between Oct. 26 and Oct. 28 by Emerson College Polling found Democratic candidate and pastor Adam Hamilton at 49% over Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, who polled at 45%. The survey, which asked voters who they would vote for if the election were held today, carried a 3.5 percentage point margin of error. Trump on Thursday canceled his weekend trip to a rally in Kansas because Marshall is “doing very well,” but reversed his plans by Friday morning and announced he’ll appear in person, as scheduled. He similarly flipped on canceling his trip to Iowa to support Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running against Democrat Josh Turek for U.S. Senate. While the U.S. House appears to be tipping toward the Democrats, only a small fraction of the races across the U.S. are competitive. The districts include California’s 22nd; Florida’s 14th and 22nd; Iowa’s 2nd; Kentucky’s 6th; Michigan’s 4th, 7th and 10th; Montana’s 1st; New York’s 17th; North Carolina’s 1st; Ohio’s 7th and 9th; Texas’ 15th and 35th; and Virginia’s 1st, according to widely cited prognosticators. Surge in early voting Tens of millions of Americans have already marched — some literally — to the polls, or submitted their mail-in ballots, in the final stretch leading up to Election Day. Carrie LeVan, a political scientist at Colby College in Maine, said she’s not sure whether the enthusiasm driving early voters will translate into a “wave” election for Democrats, like the 2010 midterm “Tea Party” wave when Republicans regained House control by flipping more than 60 seats. “There’s a lot of hype and expectation that Democrats are going to perform and have this huge wave this election cycle, and I don’t know — if I’m gonna make a prediction, I don’t think it’s gonna be that big,” she said. Early voting at Kearny Town Hall in Kearny, New Jersey, on Oct. 24, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor) LeVan highlighted this cycle’s rare mid-decade redistricting by Republicans, and then by Democrats, combined with “affective” polarization as obstacles to the size of shifts. The academic term affective polarization, she explained, is not just clinging to your side and your beliefs but rather “how much do I hate the opposition party?” “There’s all these things that have changed since the 2010 election, so can we ever have a wave that was as big, even if we’re so dissatisfied with the state of things right now?” she said. An NRP/PBS News/Marist poll published Tuesday found other possible warning signs for Democrats hoping for a big surge. The survey found several “key pillar groups” among Democratic voters, including voters under age 45 and voters of color, lagged in enthusiasm to vote in the midterms, while some Republican voter segments gained ground on who is “very closely” monitoring the races. The poll also found some swing voters turned off by the Democrats’ primary victories for some far-left candidates, including those belonging to the Democratic Socialists of America. Democrats are grappling with how to navigate the intraparty divisions, particularly if they gain control of the House. In the courts Ahead of Election Day, an array of legal challenges are playing out in federal courts across the country. The Justice Department wants to require California election officials to set aside the ballots of 20,000 voters it says are suspected noncitizens. The Trump administration doesn’t want those ballots to count unless voters can prove their citizenship. A similar request was also made to officials in Washington state. Multiple federal judges have already ruled against the DOJ’s California request and the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday dealt the Trump administration its third and fourth courtroom losses in less than a week. It’s possible the Trump administration will ask the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene. The Supreme Court on Oct. 9, 2024. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom) The Justice Department has also issued subpoenas to election officials in California, prompting a new lawsuit that seeks to stop the department from threatening state and local officials with prosecution. articles.title: Librarians are vanishing from Michigan schools just when they are needed most
articles.description: The lack of school librarians impacts students, particularly in low-income communities like Detroit and Flint and isolated ones like Alcona County in the northern Lower Peninsula and Ontonagon in the Upper Peninsula, exacerbate disparities in resources for young people.
articles.content: This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article. This story was first published in The Conversation Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools report having a school library staffed with a trained school librarian. Although Michigan strongly recommends that schools employ certified librarians, the state does not require them. In the 2023–24 school year, the state ranked 46th in the student-to-librarian ratio, with one school librarian for every 2,760 students. The lack of school librarians impacts students across Michigan, but particularly in low-income communities like Detroit and Flint and more isolated ones like Alcona County in the northern Lower Peninsula and Ontonagon in the Upper Peninsula, exacerbating disparities in resources for young people. We are scholars in library and information sciences from Wayne State University, studying information access and ethics and equity in education and school libraries. Currently, we are conducting a statewide campaign to contact every school in Michigan and learn about their libraries, staffing, book collections, technology resources and more. Michigan’s 2025–26 School Aid budget funded our statewide survey to measure the school librarian shortage and guide efforts to address it. Our work, and the work of many others, reveals how school librarians help students become strong readers and informed citizens. Fewer than 10% of Michigan public schools have a trained librarian. Harkim Wright Sr./AP Catalysts for student achievement A missing librarian is harder to see than an empty bookshelf. A room full of books can look like a school library. But if students cannot borrow those books, teachers have no librarian to plan lessons with, and no one leads author visits or digital citizenship lessons, the space offers only a fraction of what a school library can provide. School librarians bring those services to life. Also called school library media specialists, they hold a teaching certificate and complete advanced education. They connect students with books they want to read and work with teachers to build richer lessons, using library resources to extend learning beyond the textbook. Their impact stretches far beyond standardized test scores, though studies link strong library programs with higher student achievement and improved student literacy, especially for struggling readers. They can instill a love of reading and teach technological skills, which is critical in the age of artificial intelligence. At our Michigan School Census symposium held in 2026, Michigan school librarians and a principal described what that work looks like. Brian Peck, a teacher librarian at Detroit’s UPrep Academy, helped students research and build a library where none had existed. He reported that 334 students voluntarily visited and checked out books during the previous school year. At West Ottawa, librarian Julia Reynolds described replacing crowded shelves with displays that let children see book covers. Circulation quadrupled, she reported. A principal on the panel explained how district support helped schools make library visits a priority from the first week of school. Students’ information worlds Access to information is only a start. Students also need help making sense of what reaches them through searches, social media and AI. AI can create convincing fake videos of students doing or saying things they never did, harming their reputations and undermining trust in what people see online. Less visible forces shape students’ information worlds, too. Algorithms and online platforms often dictate which search results and suggested videos appear first. Students need to understand that the first result is not necessarily the most credible or trustworthy source. AI is becoming so prominent that even elementary school students are learning about it. Building information literacy Information literacy means knowing how to find, judge and use information. School librarians turn those skills into practice. For a history assignment, a librarian might help students compare a newspaper account with a firsthand record. Who produced each source? What might explain their different accounts? The same habits apply to AI. Students can trace a claim to its source, check whether the source exists and compare what it says with the generated answer. A confident response still needs evidence. Guided by certified school librarians, students can build upon these foundations and learn to effectively find, evaluate and use information, including news articles about a historic event for a social studies assignment or to analyze current social media trends. Students can also judge the accuracy, recency and relevance of information. They learn to apply information in decision-making, writing and other forms of communication. Becoming savvy digital citizens Knowing whether information is trustworthy is an important skill. Deciding what to do with it is another. Digital citizenship includes deciding whether to post someone’s photo, seeking their permission before doing so, and choosing not to share a fake video. Recent research emphasizes that digital citizenship prepares students to be empowered online and act ethically, safely and legally in digital environments. Our work also starts with the knowledge young people bring to school. Project Restoring Urban School Libraries helped classroom teachers earn the additional endorsement needed to become school librarians. The program combined mentoring with coursework that drew on students’ cultures, including using hip-hop to explore how young people find, create and share information. Students start by examining the media they already use. A lesson might ask them to trace a sample, credit its creator and discuss what changes when someone else’s work reaches a new audience. Fighting for recognition Principal preparation programs can help school leaders understand what school librarians contribute beyond book checkout. But principals and school librarians often train in separate academic units: colleges of education and schools of library and information science. Without shared coursework or joint projects, principals may complete their training without learning how to work with a school librarian. In our “Closing the Literacy Gap” symposium, we brought school librarians and administrators together on a panel to show what their partnerships make possible. West Ottawa Principal Audra Bolhuis joined school librarian Julia Reynolds and compared a librarian to “an instructional coach.” She described someone teachers can turn to for resources and help with classroom projects, extending the librarian’s role beyond students’ scheduled library visits. School library jobs remain vulnerable to budget cuts, and the number of school librarians across the state has been decreasing since 2010. To understand what schools provide and where support is missing, we launched the state-funded Michigan School Census in September 2026. By Oct. 21, 1,054 schools – about one-third of those invited – had completed it. Our public response map tracks participation across districts. Schools without libraries or librarians are essential to painting the full picture: Their staff can explain how students get books and research help when those services are absent. The findings will guide recommendations for staffing, resources and funding. Counting what schools have is the first step toward deciding what every Michigan student should be able to count on. Read more of our stories about Detroit and Michigan. Shannon Oltmann, Associate Dean of Information Sciences, Wayne State University and Kafi Kumasi, Professor of Information Sciences, Wayne State University

Mamdani's economy isn't a socialist dream or a capitalist nightmare — but his biggest bets are yet to come
articles.content: Zohran Mamdani became mayor of New York City on a simple, focused economic platform: fast and free buses, universal childcare, cheaper groceries, and a rent freeze. His supporters envisioned him ushering in a fresh economic order. His critics feared the worst — a cabal of heavy-handed leftists who would plunge the city into fiscal chaos. A year after Mamdani's election, New York's economy doesn't look like the stuff of socialist dreams — or capitalist nightmares. Zohranomics is unfolding at a piecemeal pace. Unable to unilaterally raise taxes on the rich, the mayor is championing a pied-à-terre tax on wealthy residents who don't live in the city full-time (or say so on their tax filings). His municipal grocery store endeavor is a modest five-location work in progress. The city is focused on the "fast" half of the bus plan and has put the "free" part on the back burner. Like his predecessors, Mamdani is dedicating a lot of time and resources to housing. He orchestrated a rent freeze on 1 million rent-stabilized apartments — one of his most controversial and impactful moves so far, though not unique to his administration. Many of the mayor's policy moves have been administrative measures: cutting red tape for small businesses, rooting out government inefficiencies, pension maneuvering to balance the city budget. And, the administration is trumpeting small-scale wins on filling potholes and making it easier to cancel subscriptions. The list of accomplishments sounds more like a standard Democratic think-tank wish-list than a Bolshevik manifesto. Mamdani is governing like a leftist populist with the instincts of a city operations nerd — but his biggest economic bets are yet to be made. New York is an incredibly rich city, with a private wealth pool of over $3 trillion and an annual GDP of roughly $1.3 trillion. It's also a city with stark economic divides. It has a 25% poverty rate, meaning more than 2 million New Yorkers live below the poverty line. (In comparison, the national poverty rate is 10%.) From 2019 to 2024, almost two-thirds of New York City's income growth went to the top 1%, according to the city's comptroller, compared to 39% nationally. The costs of childcare, housing, and basic necessities are increasingly daunting. Those economic dynamics propelled Mamdani to the mayorship. "A lot of people love this city, but not as many of them can live here," the mayor said in a recent podcast interview with comedian Theo Von. But the immutable truth facing any New York City mayor is that there is not much they can do to influence the economy. Much of New York's financial engine runs on its own. New York's state government sets most of the city's taxes. The national and global economies affect New Yorkers' pocketbooks, too. Mamdani's program is to, where possible, wield the city's influence to lower costs and shift some of New York's power structures toward the traditionally less powerful. That means pairing rent regulations with initiatives to stimulate more homebuilding and pressuring the state to secure funding for a new free 2-K program. The city is weighing public options where the private markets fail to deliver, such as the grocery store initiative and new government-backed property and liability insurance for landlords. It's investing $30 million into an NYU quantum computing lab in exchange for a cut of its profits. And, it's pushing the idea that the wealthy could stand to chip in more and pay higher taxes. This is a more expansive vision than a standard anti-poverty agenda — and a politically riskier one. New York is a crowded, raucous city where almost everyone sees themselves as an underdog, from billionaires to bodega owners to beleaguered renters. And when everyone feels like the system is stacked against them, any change is bound to make someone feel newly wronged. To his progressive allies, Mamdani's approach is an attempt to prove that local government can directly respond to constituents. The hope is that tackling and touting the little things, like snow shoveling and trash pickup, will build trust that they can use to address the big things. It doesn't sound as radical as socialism, says Elizabeth Wilkins, the president and CEO of the Roosevelt Institute, a progressive think tank, but it's "radical in the degree to which people have lost faith in the idea that the government cares about how they experience the economy or that the government could do anything about it." Housing is the arena where the mayor has made the biggest difference to New Yorkers on both material and rhetorical fronts. In June, the mayor-appointed Rent Guidelines Board voted to enact a two-year rent freeze on about 1 million rent-stabilized apartments in New York City, affecting an estimated 2 million residents. Meanwhile, he has advanced the argument that the root of the city's affordability crisis is a lack of housing and taken big steps to construct more. He's set out to build 200,000 more affordable homes and preserve another 200,000 over the next decade. His administration has identified city-owned land that could be turned into housing. They've created a task force to speed up affordable housing production and eliminate administrative barriers and delays, from tweaking the city's housing lottery system to reforming environmental review processes. The mayor has even nudged President Donald Trump to allow building on public sites, such as Sunnyside Yards, a rail hub in Queens. "Each change may be modest, but they are important and collectively can add up to some meaningful changes," says Ingrid Gould Ellen, a professor of urban policy and planning at NYU, of the administrative efforts. Read more of Business Insider's Cost of the City coverage Early in his tenure, Mamdani launched "rental ripoff" hearings, providing a platform for tenants to air their frustrations. It signaled to the city's renters that he's on their side and cast bad landlord behavior as both a housing-quality problem and a consumer-protection problem. Mamdani has extended an olive branch to landlords in announcing an initiative to lower their insurance costs, but the shift in priorities is making many of them feel unfairly targeted. "The tone put us on edge," says Ann Korchak, the board president of the Small Property Owners of New York. Rent freezes aren't a new idea — they were put in place three times under former Mayor Bill de Blasio on a similar number of rent-stabilized apartments. The policy's proponents point to that as evidence that the sky won't fall this time around. Its critics note that the freezes haven't curbed the upward march of the city's housing costs in the past and argue that this time would be especially detrimental, since landlords' costs are higher and increasing faster than they were a decade ago. Then there's the question of how the funding will come together for Mamdani's ambitious housing plans, and how much private developers and lenders will play ball. The rent freeze, which guarantees at least two years of flat revenues for rent-stabilized buildings, could lead to higher borrowing costs and financing challenges for builders, says Howard Slatkin, the executive director of the Citizens Housing and Planning Council. Broader economic conditions that shape financing — most notably interest rates — are entirely out of the administration's control. Building and operating housing is expensive, and "we haven't yet seen what they are thinking will move the needle on those costs," Slatkin says. Building code reform, for example, could make the math work better. The administration is looking at it, but it's a slog. Not all public land is suitable for housing, as parcels may be awkward shapes and sizes or have zoning and legal limitations. The administration has released a tracker that identifies over 100 city-owned sites it says could yield more than 50,000 homes. Some of this space isn't empty: In Bensonhurst, the city is seeking to redevelop the existing New Utrecht Library as a brand-new library plus 200 apartments. The pied-à-terre tax is a financial knock to those subject to it, but it's a minuscule part of New York's overall fiscal picture. The mayor's office estimates the tax could bring in $500 million annually, though the comptroller says it could be $340 million-$380 million, given exemptions and the likelihood some homeowners would change their behavior to avoid the tax. For context, the city's most recent annual tax revenue was $85.4 billion. Success depends on how many units are built, and their size, location, and cost. It also matters how fast construction moves, since delays are expensive. By the city's own estimate, New York needs 700,000 new homes over the next 10 years to address its housing shortage, meaning 70,000 homes a year, well above the net increase of 43,800 new units the city had in 2025. The Mamdani administration itself has acknowledged that it can take eight years for an affordable housing project to be conceived to a family actually being able to move in. It's seeking to cut eight months from the process and shrink the timeline from endeavors requiring zoning changes by two years. "To make a serious dent in our housing crisis, we need to build more quickly and efficiently," Gould Ellen, the professor, says. Mamdani has recast the deputy mayor for economic development role as deputy mayor for economic justice, a move meant to signal an administration focused on fairness, not only growth. He put in place a tenacious regulator at the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which has tried to convey that the city is willing to use its weight to address relatively mundane headaches by cracking down on bad actors in food delivery, self-storage, and even dentistry. Emily Eisner, executive director of the Fiscal Policy Institute, a progressive think tank, says she sees much of the DCWP's actions as "small potatoes" in terms of actual affordability, but there's something "symbolically important" about people seeing the government stand up for them. On small business, the administration has released 50 proposed reforms meant to cut red tape. They've also put forth ballot proposals to speed up processes for building ramps and sidewalk cafes in public spaces and reduce paperwork for city contractors. On big business, as much as Mamdani's rhetoric and political affiliation as a democratic socialist spooked some leaders, his mayoralty hasn't caused a corporate exodus. Anthropic, Fanatics, and Deloitte decided to expand in Manhattan this year. His bet is that corporations will stay and thrive in New York without City Hall bending over backward for them. "People oftentimes, even more than getting what they want, they want to feel seen and heard," Bradley Tusk, a venture capitalist, political strategist, and Andrew Cuomo ally, says. For CEOs and big business, that's not happening as it did with other administrations, Tusk says. A City Hall spokesperson points out that the mayor has put together a Business Advisory Council, hosted an international business roundtable during the United Nations General Assembly, and has held multiple meetings with prominent business leaders, including JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon and Goldman Sachs' David Solomon. New Yorkers may enjoy small financial reprieves, but the bigger challenge is bringing down the cost of bigger-ticket items. Mamdani's plan to open five city-run grocery stores is unlikely to move grocery prices significantly in a city of over 1,000 grocery stores and 10,000 bodegas and corner stores. The administration says it's chosen densely populated neighborhoods for the grocery store sites in hope of making a large direct and indirect impact on New Yorkers in those areas. Julie Samuels, the president and CEO of trade group Tech: NYC, says that Mamdani has moderated in City Hall, though he hasn't yet focused as much on job growth and economic development as administrations past. One place he has succeeded: the vibes. "Economic po

articles.title: Mamdani says Trump to grant visa to mother of boy killed in Bronx shooting
articles.content: New York City mayor says US president ‘has agreed to grant her visa immediately’. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani says after a phone call with United States President Donald Trump that the mother of a 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was shot dead in the Bronx will be granted a visa. Mamdani wrote in a post on X on Saturday that he had spoken with Trump about Javits Frimpong, whose mother is seeking to travel to New York to say goodbye to her son. The US president “has agreed to grant her visa immediately”, the mayor wrote. “The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away,” he wrote. There was no immediate comment from Trump. CCTV footage that captured the last moments of Frimpong’s life showed him being chased by three other teens on Thursday morning as he was on his way to school. He was shot in his abdomen and died the same day in hospital. Thousands of people attended vigils held for the teenager across the city. The 15-year-old had told his father he was bullied at school. Thomas Frimpong, Javits’s father, called on the police to help him “find justice for my son”. Police have said they are investigating, but no arrests have been made yet. Javits’s parents moved him to the US a year ago in the hopes of providing him a better life. Congressman Richie Torres, who represents the Bronx, wrote on social media that “our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him.” Ghanaian Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa stated on social media that Ghanaian officials are “coordinating with local authorities” and helping Javits’s mother with her visa application. Visa applications from a number of African countries have been severely limited under the Trump administration.
